div.head: `THE FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: `THE FREE CHURCHES.
DR. PARKER'S ILLNESS.

The news of Dr. Parker's fresh breakdown did not greatly surprise those who had seen him in his own house during the week preced- ing his reappearance at the City Temple. Dr. Parker was eager to get back to his work, and his friends saw that his hope of again meeting his people was buoying him up considerably. But his physical strength was still far from re- stored. He ipent the dayi mostly on his couch in his study or in the garden, and, as he told his friends, he had no desire to do anything. Even the short journey from his garden upstairs to his study tried his strength. For three score years and ten Dr. Parker has enjoyed rude, vigorous health, and like most men with such a record he is a somewhat difficult patient. His doctors find it hard to persuade him to rest completely, and his friends have no doubt that they allowed him to return to his work mainly to appease his insatiable longing to meet his people again. Dr. Parker has now been ordered to rest for six months, and if the six months were extended into twelve it would be well for him. A good suggestion that has been made is that he should spend a year on the shores of the Mediterranean and in Egypt. But whether he will follow this advice remains doubtful.

div.head: GIPSY SMITH AT THE CITY TEMPLE.
div.p: GIPSY SMITH AT THE CITY TEMPLE.

The Thursday morning service has always been very dear to Dr. Parker's heart. If it may be said of a man who is really very humble and self-depreciating it has been his especial pride. The service is being continued in the meanwhile, and was conducted the other Thursday by Gipsy Smith, the famous evangelist. He had a congregation quite as large as that which ordinarily greets Dr. Parker on a Thursday morning. It completely filled the area and overflowed a little into the gallery. Gipsy Smith's sermon on "Be filled with the spirit" was heard with the keenest attention and interest. It was the first time that he has preached in the City Temple, but not the first time that he has appeared in its pulpit, for he has on at least one occasion sung a solo there. It is certainly no disparagement *to Gipsy Smith's preaching to say that he sings almost as well as he preaches.

div.head: GIPSY SMITH'S AUTOBIOGRAPHY.
div.p: GIPSY SMITH'S AUTOBIOGRAPHY.

Gipsy Smith's autobiography, published less than a year ago by the National Free Church Council, has been an extraordinary success. The book is now in its tenth thousand, a sale which we suppose has not been reached by any religious biography for many and, many j year. The volume was published at 65., but 17e hear that a cheaper edition is in preparation, and when it appears it will no doubt be eagerly welcomed. Gipsy Smith already possesses a large public, and a public which is more intimately interested in him than in most of its other heroes and favourites, and of course as he travels over the country in the course of his evangelistic work, his public is always increas- ing.

div.head: LATE MR. KENSIT.
div.p: THE LATE MR. KENSIT.

Mr. Walter Walsh, so well known for his book on "The Secret History of the Oxford Movement," contributes an interesting sketch of the late Mr. Kensit to the November Free Church Chronicle. Mr. Walsh rightly says that "in the presence of his death all personal criticisms were silenced." Mr. Walsh remarks that he often differed in opinion from Mr. Kensit in matters of detail, but no doubt as to his perfect sincerity and honesty ever entered lois head. In private life Mr. Kensit was excesdmgly affectionate. There was un- doubtedly a great deal of "John Bull" in him, but he loved all those who loved the Lord Jesus Christ. He was in no sense a high - class orator, yet he could hold the attention a a vast audience for two hours at a time, no slight testimony to his platform power. He had a keen sense of humour, and he loved ;to tell a good story which would make people laugh. Mr. Walsh maintains that in founding the organisation known as the Wycliffe Preachers, Mr. Kensit rendered a greater service to the cause he had at heart than he did by his protests in Ritualistic churches.
THE EDT.TCATION BILL.

The autumn sitting of Parliament, which has ,now begun, is likely to be marked by scenes more stormy and dramatic than have been wit- nessed at St. Stephen's since the Home Rule days. The Premier is plainly resolved to use all the force he can command to push the Bill through. The Opposition, on the other hand, is as firmly resolved to do all that the forms of Parliament permit to prevent its passage, and it is not at all unlikely that they will be rein- forced by discontents on the Government side. The tactics to be pursued by the Irish mem- bers are still in doubt, but their ranks are being thinned by continual removals to prison, and they are in 'a frame of mind by no means friendly to the Govern- ment represented at the Irish Office by Mr. Wyndham. If the Bill should pass, the troubles of the Government will only have begun; for over 400 Free Church Councils have declared in favour of an anti-rate campaign. Assuredly these Councils and those whom they represent will not turn back, and the Government, which is engaged in selling up and imprisoning Non- conformists by the thousand, will certainly have its hands full. But the future of this matter is a deep mystery. He would be a rash man ,who would dare to prophesy.

div.head: REV. THOMAS LAW AND AMERICA.
div.p: THE REV. THOMAS LAW AND AMERICA.

The Rev. Thomas Law, the General Secretary of the National Free Church Council, has again ' been urgently invited to visit, the United Sates to develop the Federation Movement there on the lines already so well and truly laid in this country: But Mr. Law's absorbing duties in connection with the Education Campaign, and other matters, make it impossible for him to entertain the invitation—at any rate for the pre- • sent,. Probably, however, at some later period Mr. Law's services may be spared from this country for a few months in the interests of the American Evangelical Churches. We hear by the way that it is practically certain that Mr. W. R. Lane, one of the National Council's Misisioners, will undertake an evangelistic tour in South Africa next spring. There are already Evangelical Councils in Cape Town, Port Eliza- beth, King William's Town, Durban, and in other centres.

div.head: " FREE CHURCHMAN" FOR 1903.
div.p: THE " FREE CHURCHMAN" FOR 1903.

The Free churchman (National Free Church Council, Memorial Hall, London) for January, 1903, contains the first instalment of a fasci- nating serial story, entitled "St. Issey," by Joseph Hocking; a short story by Mrs. L. T. Meade ; and articles by Revs. Hr. R. F. Horton, M.A., Dr. Joseph Parker, Dr. W. J. Townsend, F. B. Meyer, 8.A., and Bernard J. Snell, M.A., B.Sc. There are two special articles, The Romance of the Daily News and "The Humours of Motoring as depicted by Punch," and several topical pages. The magazine 18 well illustrated. A feature of the issue is the coloured fine art supplement, containing choice reprecluctions of pictures by some of the great masters. The Free Churchman has an excellent programme for 1903, its contributors including eminent names in literature and in the religious and professional worlds. It is admirably adapted for localising by the Free Church The Most Nutritious.

div.head: ILLUSTRATED FASHIONS.
div.p: ILLUSTRATED FASHIONS.

There is one consoling thought which must arise through the depression produced by the terrilde climatic conditions of an English winter, namely, that though sunny skies and brilliant sunshine show to advantage the charms of early youth set in a back-ground of muslin and flowers, there is more chance for the generality of wonvenkind to appear at their best in the soft firelight or beneath the shaded lamps of a wintry afternoon or evening, clad inn warmly-tinted gown softened by some furs. Ont-of-doors the thick veil which had to be discarded in the heat of June may do ser• viceable duty in Novemlier, and by half-revealing, • half-concealing the face beneath enhance the attractions of the wearer. A woman of thirty never looks better than when dressed for the street in a dull crimson frieze gown worn with sables or black fox and a black picture hat. The crimson warms a pale complexion and softens a too highly- coleured one, while furs are always becoming : and It is well worth while when purchasing any fur

div.head: SMART COSTUME.
div.p: A SMART COSTUME.

article to wait till one can afford something really good, and avoid all the cheap rubbish which look good but wear badly, and prove most unsatisfac- tory possessions. The smart costume sketched looks well worn with somegood furs. It is of a good shade of navy blue cloth, simply but well made (for simplicity is the acme of success in a tailor- made costume), set off by a handsome sable necklet of the flat order and a muff to match. The toque is of dark blue velvet trimmed with bands of sable and boasting a long ea,che-peigne of black Chantilly lace which reaches to the waist. It is wonderful how long these depending streamers of lace and ribbon are on the most fashionable hats and toques. There are times, however, when they suggest the streamers of a widow's bonnet in a fashion not altogether pleasing. I cannot help thinking that this extreme popularity for a fashion which, to say the least of it, is decidedly nn-English, will ensure its speedy banishment from our midst. In the meantime, however, we all attach bows and streamers of ribbon velvet or silk, or figured silk scarves to the back of our hats and congratulate ourselves on ranking in the first of the modes whether the result proves a success or not. Tile Toreador hat. -however, requires some sort of am addition of this kind to soften the rather hard outlines of the round upLurned brim, which proves

trying in its severity to most faces. I have depicts in the accompanying illustration a hat which if altogether up-to-date so far as the declared mode: are concerned. It is of soft green felt, with tlu edge of the brim which is turned up at the bad bound with velvet. An irridescent buckle is placec across the front of the crown, catching into place r, soft silk scarf of emerald green figured with black which after surrounding the crown is passed round to the back of the hat, where it is tied in a bow. the long ends of which depend to the shoulders and are finished by a black chenille fringe. Instead ol stitching the folds of the scarf into place, it is securely but lightly held by a few jetted pins with ornamental heads. A careful examination of most of the French millinery models will soon prove that our sisters across the channel have adopted this method to the further success of their chapeaux.

There is something exceedingly comfortable in the feeling of one of the new felt hats in wear, as they are pliable, warm, and very light. The prettiest sort need very little trimming, for they are so exceedingly ornamental in themselves. The surface of these has a satiny gleam about it, and yet is covered with long hairs which resemble nothing so much as those of the Angora cat.

Parliament it is thought will not Vjourn until th‘? middle of December, and th.s will postpone the departure of many intending visitors to the great Durbar at Delhi until the last moment. The Duke and Dechesa of Con- naught will only take a small party. but Lord and Lady Cuizon will entertain on a large Ensle, and most of the Indian Princes, who were over hero for the coronation invited large parties to accept their hospitality in India. A great many well-known people in Society are go:ng out, iacheding the Duke and Duehese of Portland, Lord and Lady Crewe, Sir Michael and Lady Hicks-Beach, and Lord and Lady Pembroke. We should all be glad of any reliable means of keeping the moth awiy, but the " Journal of the Board of Agri- eulture " which deals with the subject in its current issue, is unable to suggest a sovereign remedy. The best advice it has to cfffr is to frequently insr sot, beat, and eh :le clothing liable to be intected. If there is no great objection to tile smell, carbon or napthalene will help to keep the adult moth away from drawers and wardrobes, and benzine may be used for furnhure, but eons of these preventives are whcl:y to be depended upon. If the eggs have been deposited in the material aotking in the ordinary way will prevent them hatebing, except beating and shaking them out, and when once the lame have obtained possession of such articles as bedding and upholstery, which cannot well be treated in this way, it is best to have it destroyed. We frequently sally forth to inspect the shop win- dows, but we have net yet arrived at the American custcm of freely going it:Leeds to see what they contain. There are exceptional occasions, but as a rule, we do not venture inside, save with the idea of purchasing something. The shopwalker at once requests to know the department one requires, and be would probably begin to think of the police, if told that on* simply wanted to look about. One mast say that one is requir- ing something, when one is forthwith conducted to a high chair and the salesperson who serves these particu- lar goods. Tbe American "women en the other hand considers herself free to enter any store without being cateehised in this way, and she very often resents our methods ef shopping in We country. In some of the big establish- ments of New York, there is not only a nursery with toys, and nursemaids to look after the ehildren but also a band, reading room, and other attractions, in addi- tion to the display of the latest fashions in gowns, hate, and chiffon. One may spend an agreeable morning in ratting through some trifling amount of shopping,and it certainly has its advantages over our system which, unless a purchaser, limits one to gazing in the shop windows. Full skirts, with the pleats stitched flat from the waist, or a tightly fitting hip piece, to the knees, from whence they are permitted to flew ow, are meeting with much approval among modistes, but so far their customers they say, show a decided preference for either the circular skirt with one seam down the front, and an almost plain back, or the familiar seven-gored skirt, which is at once so light and graceful. Much as lb. dressmakers approve of the kite, the hip piece is not becoming to the generality of women. It cuts the figure up and takes from the height, moreover pleats, however well stitched and pressed, are bulky, save in the thinnest fabrics. Regarding colours, green is the favourite of the moment. Blue may not be mixed with it, this combination having been done to death, but tho intreenetion ef either grey or In two is quite permissible. M. Worth is, it appears, building the (quite short walking skirt, so lesser lights will possibly soon be following his lead. To find oneself with two needs at liberty, when taking one's walks abroad, is a luxury that has long been denied us, but now the ooncessien is made we are not likely to easily relinquish it. The correct cut is at least two inches off the ground all remnd, and the skirt should belt out well at the hem. M. Worth is favouring tartans considerably for welkiog gowns, sometimes the entire costumes being fashioned of them, but more frequently they are used as trim- mings. The home worker should beware of thetas fabrics. They need skilful and experienced fingers to deal successfully with them, otherwise they appear dowdy in the extreme. Little three tier capes—the lowest reaching midway between shoulders and waist, the pointed front falling almost to the knees, are being worn with many smart afternoon toilette'. They have no collar, the neck being slightly eloped away, a mode followed in the cut of all , outdoor coverings this autumn. Usually, the material ' employed matches that of the gown, lace, fringe, pas- sernenterie long pendant tassels and dangling things in general, appearing en these little coverings,which taken altogether, are a welcome change from the popular abort sac Goatee. Women who are going to India for the Delhi Durbar are now rejoicing that many of the airy-fairy frocks provided for our summer—which never came—are still In their warpings of silver paper, just as they came from the dressmaker. Scarcely any alterations will be necessary, and much expense will thus be saved over the outfit. Gowns of Irish lace, or Venetian points, evens in every order for the Durbar, and ita attendant festivities, while for Egypt and the South of Franeseace gowns are in great requeet. We should all, however,do well to bear in mind the fact that the rule which applies to velvet applies to lace, namely, it mutt bt good,or nut employed at all. Some years ago, Lady Cohn Campbell translated from the French a little book entitled " The Lady's Dressing Room," which contained many uietul recipes and hints for preserving our appearaneo. Amongst other sugges- tions for retarding the coming of wrinkles, WWI the recommendation to frequently reverse the usual method of weshing the face. Always washing the face with the same motion and pressure will help to develop the lines which nature will insist on placing there. but a reversed motion will tend to smeotte them out. Washing and drying the face from the temples towards the nose will tend to keep away crow's feet round the eyes, and inatead of the usual stereotyped way, washing the face from the bottom to the tep, will help in keeping the countenance from being prematurely stamped with lines. It is a simple but very reasonable piece of advice, which every woman would do well to follow, no matter what her age may be.

div.head: PRETTY BLOUSE.
div.p: PRETTY BLOUSE.

Various festivities are even by now looming on the social horizon of most of us: so this suggestioa for a pretty evening blouse will not come amiss. There are various ways in which it might be ex- pressed, but perhaps the one which would wear longest is that in which black net plays a promi- nent part, made over a slip of black or white silk. The bodice part is a succession of tucks, while a lace berthe finishes the decolletage. In the centre front a pink conventional poppy is arranged. Across the shoulders pass two straps of pink velvet rib...ft to match the poppy (though black could be substituted if preferred) finishing in a bow on the top of the left shoulder. From a band of lace and ribbon the loose sleeves depend, leaving the upper part of the arm bare, and are caught again at the wrists by another twist of ribbon and lace An old evening bodice or an afternoon blouse of delicate colour could soon be adapted to form the slip underneath, and the net blouse could be altered in colour to harmonise or contrast well with the lining. Instead of black a rose pink net blouse over white, finished with creamy lace and trimmings of black velvet ribbon and a black poppy would be exceedingly smart wear. Indeed, those of us who look forward to a gay winter should toke time by the forelock and make ap a 4slnty blouse such as this without delay. Osforms,

div.head: [ALL RIGHTS RhSERVED.]
div.p: [ALL RIGHTS RhSERVED.]
SISTER SERATIIINE,
JULIAN CORBETT, (Author of " A Business in Great Waters," ckc.)
PART 11.
VIII.

Father Andrew was still young enough to have retained his later enthusiasms. For the most part they were orderly and disciplined. The Church, of course, held the first place; for her his enthusiasm was loving and entire. is other emotions were mainly deductions from this. Indeed, there was but one intemperance of opinion that he permitted himself, and that was an unassailable confidence in his own tact. It is not too much to say that this was the only aspect in which he recognised his indi- viduality ; otherwise he was content to regard him- self as a mere detail in the stupendous machinery of the Church. There was something so grandly humble in this conception of his existence that it satisfied his self-esteem ; nor did his diplomatic ability interest him beyond its applicability to the necessities of the Church.

It was, then, with a feeling of considerable exal- tation that Father Andrew set out on his mission. As he passed the lodge, Sergeant Poiton was assembling for a new operation on the perch. He was already standing to arms with his bamboo rod, and Madame Poiton was in motion across the cause- way with his stool, his umbrella, his bait-box, and. other details of the train.
"You are going to fish, Sergeant ?" said Father, Andrew, in a patronising tone. "Yes, Father," answered the Sergeant, gravely. "We must each catch what we can for her."

It-must be that the -Sergeant waa. jealous of the-Jesuit. It was far too sunny to hops for a.toite,.even under the shade, of the willows, but. knowing Father Andrew was bent upon Sister Seraphineawork.he could not rest idle. It would be •wrung,too, to say he did not admire his rival. He had, indeed, a very high sense of his talents, =1 ,as with shaded eyes he stood watching the black-:figure growing rapidly smaller down the long causeway and melting into the shadows that made bars of blue across the gleaming stones,. he could fancy the poplars drew themselves up to the " Present " to salute the Jesuit as he passed. By the time the priest was out of sight, Madame Poitonhad arranged the stool on the spot by tho old willow, where the Sergeant had long ago worn, the grass quite bare, and he began his vigil- Presently, imthe sunny stillness, an ox wagon, laden with rushes, came creaking up out of the marsh. The blue-bloused peasant stopped when he came. level with the fisherman, and while the lazy oxen wearily tried to brush away the gad-flies he crossed the causeway wiping his moist brow. "Any sport, Sergeant?" said he. "Not yet," said the Sergeant. " Ah, one must be patient at that work." "I am trying to get a perch for the Mother. To- morrow is Friday, you know." " Ah, that is fine work. Finer than carting litter for her cows."
"'We must each do what we can for her,'' answered the Sergeant with chastened pride, and as the cart toiled on again in the sand its labouring music was very pleasant in his ears.

div.head: LX.
div.p: LX.

Father Andrew found the Baron in his study. He was a tall handsome man of middle age with an air of dissipation that became his dryness well. His moustache, perhaps, boasted its education too. flagrantly for perfect good tone, but otherwise he. was undeniably distinguished, and might have. passed for an Englishman of the type now uni- versally recognised, admired, and imitated on the continent. Indeed, one of his secret satisfactions was that a newly-appointed British Minister had once addressed him by mistake in English.

He had just unpacked a pair of hainmerless guns which had arrived from London, and as the priest entered he was fondling them with the same sense of delight that another man might feel for a Japanese sheath-knife or a Meisonnier. The snap of the parts, as he put them together, sang to him of perfection, and he caressed their smooth brown surfaces with a pleasant sense of the extreme of human possibility. The Jesuit, who knew some- thing of perfected instruments, could not help admiring tools so admirably adapted for their pur- pose. "Are they not perfect? ".said the baron, in recep- tion of the priest's diplomatic eulogy. "An extraordinary people these English." "Most extraordinary," answered the priest. "They perfect everything but themselves." "They have no Church, you see," said the Baron, dryly. " True ; but from you I was hardly prepared for such ao explanation. "Perhaps it isn't one," said the Baron. "Perhaps not," said the Jesuit, good humour- edly. "I know the Church professes to explain every- thing," the Baron went on, as though bent on disturbing the suave gravity of his guest. "May I explain my Visit?" said the Jesuit, determined not to be ruffled by the other's sneers. "I came on behalf of the Little Sisters of Pain."

• The Baron burst out laughing. "The Little Sisters of Pain !" he cried. " Excuse my smiling, but you God-worshippers are so droll. You have no sense of humour. Little Sisters of Paint What a name! I'll bet you now, Father, there are many would have made very pretty little daughter' of pleasure. Come, am I not right?" "My dear Baron," said Father Andrew, a little disturbed. "This is really not the point of view for which I came here to ask your considers - tine."
_ "I know, I know. You want to hear if lam serious in the proposal I laid before your little abbess."

"Exactly, if you put it that way." "Well, i am. I can tell you that at once. A. pretty woman has no more right to shut herself up out of sight than the sun has not to shine." "My dear baron, surely this is going too far. Consider her position." "I have. I recognise no difference between Sister Seraphine and any other beauty, except what the Church has made, and the distinctions of the Church were always too subtle for me. She is a beauty, isn't she, Father? She promised to be at seventeen."

"Really, Baron, you must not expect me to discuss the personal attractions of a nun. I must beg you to consider the case seriously for a moment. You know the lady has been practically cloistered for many years. An interview with such a person would amuse you no doubt. But you have otter amusements. To her it, would be inexpressibly painful." "Oh, you needn't expect me to behave that, Father. I don't find it is the way with women. They like me, and I like them. Besides, I have no amusements which amuse me, and I am quite taken with this idea. Your little abbess they say is the prettiest woman in the province and I mean to have a ate-et-tgte with her if I can."

"But even if she would consent, the Church would never permit it." "Oh, of course, that is another thing. If the Church finds insuperable obstacles to my selling the hospital to the Sisters, why, of course, the Sisters must go. But I don't think the Church will.. It is not its way to find objections insuperable." "I assure you, Baron, yfou have too great faith in the power of the Church." "Perhaps. It is a. respectable excess at any rate. Still, I should never have expected you to admit I had faith in anything." You know what I mean, Baron. It is impossible. I could not even bring such a proposi- tion before Monseigneur." "Well, that is your affair. But you need not be afraid. I fancy it would take a deal to shock Monseigneur." " Baron ! Baron! you are really too hard on us. Once more let me urue you to consider what you

are aoing. How can you as a gentleman put a lady in this painful position?" Father Andrew was getting desperate. " That is my affair, sir," retorted the Baron, sharply. "It amuses me." " Very well," said the priest, rising, and with difficulty suppressing his indignation, "I will not urge you further. I see you are determined to persist in your ungentlemanlike course. In your own house I cannot express myself more plainly." "Oh, say what you like," said the Baron, with a laughing sneer. "But it is hardly worth your while. A Jesuit's opinion or, what is honourable has long been a matter of indifference to me." The Jesuit rose stiffly to depart, and then paused a montent. "You are inexorable," said he. "One nfust be amused," said the Baron, touching the hell, and the defeated diplomatist went out. _ _ .

His pace was heavy and his head hung low as he passed back along the causeway in the evening light. Sergeant Poiton had done his fishing and was standing looking down the road. The tops of the long row of poplars were sharp against the dull glow of the sky, and somehow now they seemed drawn up sternly with fixed bayonets, and Father Andrew showed dimly like a prisoner that marched between. _ _

"YOU have been successful, Sergeant?" said the priest, as he reached the spot where the porter stood waiting. "I have caught a perch for the Mother," said the Sergeant. "II wish I were as good a fisherman," answered the priest. "We must all do what we can," answered the Sergeant in triumphant humility, and Father Andrew passed on in complete dejection.

Sister &raphine was hardly disturbed at her director's failure. From the very first she knew the ordeal would come. She knew he would fail, and she had 'hardened.herself for her martyrdom. Her only desire was that the trial should not be delayed long. "There is nothing, then," she said, severely, when Father Andrew had told her that the Baron would not be denied his, amusement, "nothing but to apply to Monseigneur for permission." "Nothingbut that," answered the Jesuit, " hope- less as it is. .

"Then I will. write to him at 'once," said Sister Serapiaine. "I trust," cried the 'Jesuit in alarm, "you will do nothihg so precipitate. It is a matter that requires the utmost tact and delicacy. Monseigneur might misinterpret your anxiety." A crimson flush upon, the beautiful face, and a look of pain past words, were the only answer Father Andrew had. Sister Seraphine had never thought of it like that before.

"Ave Maria! Thou who art stainless show me my heart ! " On the faldstool before the Madonna in her little room Sister Seraphine prayed in an agony. Was it as the Jesuit had said? Was it that which gave her courage to.-wait so calmly for her trial! She prayed but hardly desired her prayer; fear- ing to see•right down into her heart for the sin she might find. there. She prayed, for she could do nothing else. She could not bear to go amongst the children. They, at least, were pure, and she—Heaven knew what sinful desire was in her. So she tortured her stainless soul as she had been taught to do from her girlhood, till she began to be sure what the Jesuit feared was true, and the prospect of the ordeal was too horrible to think of. What was left, if her purity was gone I To find this she had renounced everything. She had it in her mind to go to the novices, and tell them all the truth, and warn them before it was too late to go back to their homes, where alone it was possible to be good. Far into the night she prayed, not daring to think, "Ave Maria. Thou who art stainless, cleanse my heart !"

div.head: XI.
div.p: XI.

Monseigneur pooh-poohed the whole affair over his coffee. For Father Andrew's better educa- tion—for he was a promising young man—he affably explained to him how ridiculous he was. Gracefully gesturing with the butter knife, he pointed out that not only was the proposed interview without precedent and impossible, but it was impolitic in the extreme. The enemies of the Church were always on the watch for a scandal and to allow a tete-d-I(3te between Sister Seraphine and so notor- ious a rout; as the Baron was simply to play into their hands. "At the same time," observed his eminence," the Hospital at Ghoulines is undoubtedly doing wonders for the clerical cause for miles round. It is worth an effort to save. I will, therefore, go and see the Baron myself. You must not mind having failed with such a man. He is quite beyond your calibre. I will go myself and bring him to reason." That was how Monseigneur's coachman to his serious astonishment came to be driving out of the old city, where the Belfry is reflected in the canal and the roofs make sharp red angles against the sky, with orders, to conduct his eminence to the Chateau Blamburg. The Baron was delighted with Monseigneur, and so was Monseigneur with the Baron. He even stayed to dinner. But it was done before Mon- seigneur had made much progress with his errand. He had told all his best stories. The Baron had listened to them with real enjoyment. Monseigneur had pleasantly refused to listen to the Baron. Still, as I say, little progress had been made. Alter dinner they went into the garden to take coffee in the Kiosk where is the view of the famous Belfry at the end of the long stretch of canal.- Here Monseigneur re-opened the attack, but the Baron blew away in the smoke of his cigar every- thing Monseigneur projected at him, and progress was slower than ever. Monseigneur coaxed, argued, implored, and even threatened, but feeling at once his mistake, he took another sip of brandy and told a new story. Still the Baron was inexorable. "But the whole thing is absurd," said Monseig- neur. "I wonder you can't see that."

"That is what amuses me so much," answered the Baron, smoking imperturbably. "You can surely see that." "But you will not understand," persisted the other, "that I have no power to grant such a dispensation." "I suppose you can refer the case to Rome." "My dear Baron, that is too ridiculous." "Oh, I quite see the humour of it. It would be a joke against you in the College for the rest of your life. I shall amuse them at the Jockey Club, immensely." "But you can't seriously intend to persist in an attitude which will "

"My dear Monseigneur, I never allowed the prudery of a woman to stand in the way of my enjoyment; I am not likely to now." "I assure you Baron, that nothing was further rom my though:ts than, to suggest anything so rivial—of course, we don't ask that." "But Father Andrew made rather a point of it."

7-- "lie has seen so little. I was about to impress upon you the excellenee of the institution that your persistence must bring to an end." "Oh, I should be really sorry for that." ' "But don't you see it must come to that?" "No, Monseigneur, no! I don't think it will come to that. No more do you. Let us talk of something else. It is nearly time for you to go, and we are boring each other with all this." But Monseigneur would not tell any more stories, and his "good.eight " had something stately and cold in it.

div.head: XII.
div.p: XII.

Monseigneur was a worldly monseigneur, but that did notlaffeet his loyalty. He feared nothing so much as ridicule, but that had no effect on the courageous performance of his duties. Though no longer young like Father Andrew, he still allowed the Church the first claim on his conduct. In her interest, as he had said; the Ghoulines Hospital was worth an effort to save, and as his carriage rattled over the uneven pavement of the old city, past the proud belfry, and into the gabled square where the grass grew amongst the stones and his florid palace stood, he resolved to make that effort.

That night Monseigneur in his slippers referred the case to Rome : and though next morning he rose with a feeling of pleasant elevation, as the days went by, the sacrifice he had made caused him to sit uneasily, and he could not conceal frOm him-, self that his appetite was not at all the thing. At the Vatican the case aroused more attention than the interests at stake seemed to call for. At the Jockey Club M. de la Course was always ready to give the exact state of the market about the Abbess and the Baron. At the Hospital Sister Seraphine was on her

anees—annost always on her knees—praying for whet: That was what was hardest, even prayer was denied her. For the dispensation she dared not pray. "He might misinterpret your answer." Father Andrew's words seemed written on her brain—to pray for the dispensation was too like the desire she feared. To pray that it would never come, that was to pray away the work of her life and long misery to the Sisters and the children. Silly little Sisters of Pain ! What a pity thee Baron could not know how ridiculous you were I It would have been a distinct gain to the joke. '

div.head: XIII.
div.p: XIII.

The Baron's simple faith in the power of the Church received no shock. In due course the dis- pensation came from Rome. Monseigneur's appetite returned, and he sent in the dispensation to Sister Seraphine with quite a pleasant little note conzratulating her on the success which had attended his Mints on her behalf. "It was a serious step to take," he wrote, " a grave responsibility to assume, but believe me, in behalf of so excellent an institution I do not regret what this ha&cost me." "It will be terrible," shuddered Sister S4raphine, as she handed the letter to her counsellor. "Yet it is better to suffer in this world than to die =- purged of sin." "The good God knows," sighed Sister Thiodore "Yet I would have thought a lighter penance was enough for your sins, Mother." "Hush I Sister," exclaimed the other. "You don't know; you don't know." But Sister Theodora thought she did.
(To be concluded.)

div.head: JUDGMENTS AGAINST WORKMEN
div.p: JUDGMENTS AGAINST WORKMEN
Mr. F. Monks at the Wigan County Court.

At a recent sitting of the Wigan County Court,certain judgment summonses against workmen employed by the Monks, Ball and Steal Works, Aspull, were adjourned for tho purpose of obtaining evidence as to the means of the defendants, it having been said by the gents for the plaintiffs that the company had declined to forward the usual certificate for men's earnings. _ _ _ .

A subpoena was issued upon Mr Frederick Minks, of Walton Old Hall, Warringten,a director of the company, to attend befrre his Honour Judge Bradbury, at the W igan County Court, on Tucsday, and produce the wage books of the company. His Honour, addressing Mr Monks, said he had a strong objection to sending lawn to prison unless he had absolutely accurate information with regard to their wages. and under the powers of the Court he was eatitled to get information from the cm; !osiers. .To avoid dragging employers into court it was customary to ask them to send returns af their wages, and the course had worked exceedingly well. He understood that it had been stated the information which was sup- plied was shown to outsiders, but he assured Mr Monks that that was absolutely untrue. Mr Monks said he saw the reasonableness of the course, and in future the company would give all the informa- tion possible. Be apologised for any de!ay which had arisen•

Mr Allen, solicitor, representing Megsrs Monks, Hal, and Co., said the company had never intended any dis- respect to the court. He explained the matter to them, and, therefere, there would be no further troulle. Mr Monks undertook to rotund 27e 9,1 costs incurred by the creditor to secbre the witnesses' attendance. His Honour thanked Mr Monks for the course he had taken.

div.head: Humorous Contest at Parr Hall.
div.p: Humorous Contest at Parr Hall.

Humour held sway at Parr Hall on Monday evening, when the sixth runnel contest promoted by Messrs Kilduff and flardiman took piece. That these competitions are very popular with Warring- ton people was evident from the large audience, almost every seat being occupied. Seventeen humorists competed and their songs and sketches occasioned great hilarity. The judge was Mr H Ballard, and considering that there was only a margin of seven points between the first prize winner and the competitor who was ,awarded the fifth prize, the task of adjudication was by no means easy. Mr Alfred Rearle, of Levenshul ' ose secured the first prize for his " IriA.stories " which created unbounded mirth. The second prize, of £3, was awarded te Mr Frank Lauri, of Stockport, for a sketch entitled " The amateur orchestra," the third avrird of £2 was secured by Mr Fred llorsfall, of Leeds, who gave" Moriarty's Birthday," the fourth prize of .£1 was Riven to Mr Fred Walmsley, of I.3alford ; and the fifth, of 10s, went to Mr A Croxon, of Leeds. The other competitors were Mr Charles Mowarth, of Leeds; Messrs Mark Tyme,Manchester; Flank Hale, Miles Platting; Walter Wade, Leeds ; A B Millard, Manchester ; Joe Harwood, Bolton ; To Oliver, Nelson ; T Barney, Sheffield ; Harrison Hall, Manchester ; Tich Thomas, Warrington ; Tom Gregory, Warrington; and Bert Parratt,Manchester. Mr Matt Kilduff, lent additional interest to the programme by his laughable song " Patent medicir advertisements," and Mr W Kilduff displayed con- siderable ability as an elocutionist, Mr Albert Holt, of Manchester, was an efficient accompanist.

Die man Coorad,who was convicted for conspirieg to get an impression of the keys of pillar-boxes in London. was on Tuesday sentenced to two years bard labour. It was stated that the gang if which hs was a member had robbed several boxes, keeping any cheques they might find and substituting forged ones, which they for warded to their destination in the same envelopes. A senior gentleman cadet at the Royal Military College, Sarmhurst, was summarily dismissed after dinner on Monday night. He was in "F" Company, and after changing into raufti, vas mart hed betweets all the cadets lined up in the corridors. On either side or him was a senior officer, while Captain Knox walked behind. He was taken to the gates of the CcLege sad thee diarnisaed.

div.head: NEW ROMAN CATHOLIC
div.p: THE NEW ROMAN CATHOLIC
CHURCH.
Opening of St. Mary's, Latchford.

An interesting and important event in the history of Roman Catholicism in Warrington took place on Sunday, when the Lord Bishop of Shrewsbury (the Right Rev Dr Allen) opened the new Church of St Mary at Latchford. It is interesting to mete that St Mary's, Latchford, is the second oldest Roman Catholic Mission in the Borough. It was opened some forty years ago in the old cotton mill in St James'-street and served by the Rev Father Alcock. from Altrinchain, About thirty-five years ago Father Alcock acquired the site in St Mary's street and erected a school-chapel. The Rev P Mulvaney was then appointed resident priest. Three years ago the schools were pronounced by the Education Department as insufficient for the accommodation of the children in attendance. This necessitated the present Rector, the Rev Father McGrath, entering upon the undertaking of build- ing a new church, the foundation stone of which was laid by the Bishop of Shrewsbury on August 11th of last year. The work has progressed very rapidly under the supervision of the builder, Mr Peter McLachlan, of Birkenhead, and Sunday witnessed the opening services. The Church, which is of transitional Gothic style of architecture, has been bnilt from the designs of Mr Robert Curran, C.E., of Warrington, and stands at the corner of St Mary-street and Clifton-street, ad- joining the schools (used as a chapel) and the pres- bytery, to which it is attached. The church will provide accommodation for 600 people, the main entrance being from St Slary-street, although there is another entrance from Clifton-street, through the tower. The exterior, which is very imposing, is faced with Yorkshire stone parpoints, with red dressings. The length of the church is 124 feet, the width 53 feet, and the height to the ceiling 50 feet. It is intended at some future time to erect a tower and spire rising to a height of 150 feet. The interior of the church is very handsome, there being a nave and two side aisles. There are two side chapels, and a large and lofty sanctuary. The choir accommodation is provided in a gallery over the main entrance, and is reached by a turret staircase. The baptistry is placed at the endof the nortblaisleosear !o the main entrance.and the vestry accommodation is en the north side,hnv- ing communication with the presbytery by a cloister. The heating chamber adjoins the veetries• The elereetory is supported by polished massive granite columns with bases and caps of Yorkshire stone, the arches being built of red atone. There are two niches at the entrance to the sanctuary. above which springs the heavily moulded chancel arch rising to a height of 40 feet. The sanctuary is divided from the nave by a white polished marble step. The lighting is very satisfactory. The aisles are lighted by ten two-light tracery headed windows and the clerestory by twelve three-light tracery headed windows. Each of the side chapels has a wheel window at the end. The sanctuary is lighted by four two-light windows,and there is also a large tracery window at the west end, iromed- eje_

It was es the end of one book and the beginning of another. It was almost 30 years ago to the dap that he stood in the place of his Bishop, who was unable to cisme, and preaehed the first sermon in the school-shapel. They bad been able to leave behind, as it were, the school chapel, in itself unworthy, and to commence their worship in that beautiful new building. They had raised up a temple for Gad, and their joy had increased day by day as the building had grown in size and beauty. In it they could now offer their worship to God, and give Him their loyal service, Pontificial Benediction was celebrated in the evening the clergy present being :—The Lord Bishop, Canons Craig and Callow, Fathers Giles, Chambers, McGrath, and D'Arcy. div.head: NORTHERN RUGBY LEAGUE.
div.p: THE NORTHERN RUGBY LEAGUE.
First Division.
WARRINGTON OBTAIN A POINT AT HALIFAX.

Warrington journeyed to Halifax on Saturday with a full team and a strong determination to check the all-conquering career of the "blue and whites." They failed to win but they did the next best thing and gained the honour of being the first team to take a point out of Halifax. Dry weather favoured the fixture and there was a big crowd of 9,080 to witness the game. The home team bad two changes from the selected side,but there was little difference in the quality of the men. _Joe Riley and Morton replaced Wedgwood and

Hammond. Mr W. M' Cutebeon. of Oldham, was the referee and the teams lined out as follows : Halifax : Little; Joe Riley, Rizg. Williams, and Hadwen ; Morley and Nettleton ; Riley, Bartle. IKorton, Wilson, Bal- mer, Iforbury, eurnmerskill, and Swinbank. Warrington : Knight; Wish Isherwood, Dickenson and Harris ; Burgess and Hockenball ; Morrison, Boardman , Forster, Edmondson, Swift (W). Swift (F), Taylor, and Roberts.

Warrington lost the toss and Taylor started against a ugh breeze. Nettleton replying to Hoekerthall who placed the hat ' in touch. Warriegton were penalised for " feet-up "In the first scrum and Little kicked beyond the centre, where Fish missed his catch and lost ground. Morrison came away smartly frona the rack and dribbled to Little whom he upset. Halifax enickly got possession from the scrum, where they had the advantage in weight, Nettleton. Rigg and Joe Riley passing aerots,the latter being held by Fish. Another penalty fell to Halifax and Little tried for goal, but placed outside. Play was of a very keen description. both sides straining every nerve. Warrington had rather the worst of matters but depended grandly. Knight finding touch at centre from one of Little's ponderous kicks. Halifax came dawn again with short passing and J Riley was only just held up at the corner. A keen struggle took place on the Warrington line, Hockenhell, Forster and Taylor eventually clearing with a fine dribble. Little got another penalty in front of the goal and failed once more, Warrington next carrying play into the Halifax half by smart work. Heckenball broke clear away from the scrimmage and with Harris in attendance ran down to Little. A score seemed cer- tain when Hockenhall passed, but the ball missed the wing man and went in touch. Warrington now attacked but were finally driven back by long punting. Fish and Dickenson got away but a pass forward spoiled a premising movement. Halifax drove Warrington balk with a forward rush which I was plualtily stopped by Dickenson. Knight was next called aspen and saved well, Warrington clearing out the invaders hv good passing between Burgess, Houlcanhall, and Harris. Halifax were back again in a moment, and Harris had to make a flying kick among the spectators to save front Morley The next minute Knight had his kisk charged down on the line, and "%We had a try at his mercy' Hesitation was fatal for Flab dashed up and held him fast right on the rut. A great effort between the two packs followed, and Warring- ton getting the ball, Burgess kicked safely into touch. Half time, no score.

Little restarted the game with a punt in toulh at the War- rington quarter, but Harris changed the venue with a smart run and punt, Fish following suit and catching the ball from his own kick It looked odds on him sailing in but Jae put his foot in touch. Warrington showed any amount of dash, and a grand run by Dickenson resulted in him capturing , Little with the ball, Warrington attacked with great vigour brit Halifax escaped by the aid of the uenal penalty. War- rington were not to be denied however, and Isherwood pick- ing op ran through only to hesitate when opposite Little and lose a glorious chance. Once again were Warrington penalised when on the attaek, and luck seemed against them. Halifax made a rush to the ether end, Joe Riley again causing trouble to the defence. Burgess relieved, Isherwood pulling Williams down at centre. Forster I next fielded smartly from al Halifax punt, and getting up speed he and Burgess ran right through the Halifax defence with well-judged transfers which, of course, went wrong en the line. Halifax cleared Warrington out with a long dribble, but the visitors were not to be denied Fish failed by inches to cross at the earner for Hockenhairs kick. Halifax got back again once more and Warrington b ing penalised, Little kicked a goal six minutes from time. There was tremendous cheering froth the borne crowd. Warrington log no time and soon had Halifax on their line again. Bur- gess. Isherwood, end Fish passing across, but to no purpose. Hockenhall cross-kicked again. and Fish appeared to get over but the touch-flag went up. Strenuous exertions were made and Warrington forwards heeled out. Burgess picked up and with a aveonderful drop-kick landed a goal from near touch, to the joy of the Warringtonians. Halifax were sorely disappointed, but Warrington well-deserved the point. They attacked to the close, when the score was 1 goal (2 points) each.

div.p: RUNCORN v. SWINTON.

A great number of spectators journeyed from Widnes, Warrington , and the surrounding districts, there being 4,0J0 present when the teams entered the enclosure Runcorn ware handicapped by the abseace of Jolley, Swinton turning out as advertised, Ruucorn.—S Houghton, back ; Jones,Bu*terworth,Warder, and Moran, three-quarter backs ; Wichardson and Foster. halt backs ; Walker, Farmer, Woods, Moulton, Higgins, Dixon, Gayter. and W. Referee, Mr F Turner, Warrington. Touch judges, Messrs E Gordon, Widnes, and Mr F Little, St Helens. Swinton started and play settled for a time at raid-field A fine passing movement saw Swinton on the Runcorn lines, Houghton having to kick dead to avoid score- The leather was quickly tent back, where Morgan mullel, letting the home team In A free kick to the visitors bronght relief.rutterwm tb marking. Warning to their work the Linnets and by a magnificent; forward mill found touch with the visitors 25 where a trot attack was kept up. Shortly afterwards Swinton were pena- lis Houghton having a futile shot at goal The game after this opened out finely Swinton gaining possession repeatedly from the scrums, but though combining splendidly they were too well watched to do any mischief. The visitors still maintained the upper hand Richardson having to kick dead. Runcorn scow began to combine with more vigour, Swinton having to defend in turn. & seeum at midfield at length gave the home team their opportunity. Forster beautifully gathered out of the serum and headed to Walker. This player threw to Warder who, after a splendid run returned to Walker who scored, Farmer converted. After this Swinton attacked very strongly, Runcorn haying to defend. r reaklng sway at length, a splendid combined effort saw Swinton pinned within tbeir lines the merest luck averting a score. On the whole Swinton were playing the best game nothing but the finest defensive work on Runcorn's part averting disaster. O'evera I spasmodic bursts saw the Swinton line in danger but the efforts lacked finish. The Linnets were not to be denied, however, A magnificent forward rush initiated by Walker saw Janes gather the ball with the line at his mercy; the leather being grounded at the corner. Houghton failed to convert from an awkward angle,Hardly had the leather i-eon set in motion when Butterworth after a splendid run threw to Walker who scored beneath the post. Farmer easily con- verting. Half time : Runcorn, two goals, three tries ; Swinton, nil.

The restarti saw the earns open a trills less swiftly though keen. Both teams visited each other's linos alternately. Over and over again the visiting team rushed to the line Only to be met by the most stubborn defence. After a furious attack Runcorn were penalised. Valentine kicking a penalty goal. Swinton still maintained the pressure. Cooper almost effecting a score. The Linnets contented themselves with defensive tactics occasionally making a brief incursion into the Lions' quarters. Try as they would the home team could not gain possession the visitors gathering repeatedly and combining beautifully. Houghton was however always to the fore and saved over and over again in fine style. Moran had a splendid chance to break away but failed to rise to the ociasion.—Final : Runcorn, two goals, thee° tries; Swin ton one pmalty goal.

ENTERIC IN ROCHDALE.
Commercial Travellers' Exposure to Infection.

Commercial travellers run considerable risk in the pursuit of their business, though it is not one that is officially classed as dangerous. They spend the greater number of their working hours in travelling In draughty railway carriages, and are continually in danger not only of accident but of exposure to infection. It is, of course, a punishable offence for anyone suffering from infectious disease to travel in a public conveyance, but it is a piece of wickednees that is often practised unde- tected, as none know better than commercial travellers —often to their cost.

Hostilities subsequently raged near mid-field, where several scrimmages took place. Hind made a good opening for Brooks, but that player passed wildly when a try seemed Certain. Burton opened the scoring for Warrington after a good rifh, the goal kick failing. The Wanderers' backs got going. but their passing was too erratic to be of any avail. Warrington were now having all the play. and Watkins scored a second point, the attempt at goal being again unsuccessful. Claim for Money Lent. At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, Elizabeth Moore, 6, Howley-lane, claimed from Charles Day. 67, Bostock-streer, the sum of £5 which she alleged was borrowed from her by the defendant and had net been paid back.—Mr Browne appeared for the plaintiff and Mr Steel defended. —Mr Browne stated that defendant's wife died in 1899, and defendant borrowed £5 for the funeral expenses. The money had never been refunded.— The defence was that defendant arranged to work ter plaintiff's husband in the bicycle repairing business to pay off the debt. He worked for plain- tiff for several months, and was ultimately dis- charged. Some money was tben owing to him. A remarkable accident occurred on the railway at Tredegar on Wednesday. A largo steam crane was being removed from the Tredegar Iron Company's works, and had to pass beneath a bridge over wnich the London and North-Western line passes. The crane came in violent contact with the bridge, an iron structure, and wrenched it from its supports. Passenge? traffic be- tween:Tredegar and Sirbosey is interrupted, and aumeral trains are entirely eusraded till the bridge can be met.

A well-known Rochdale " commercial " who was dis- cussinethis matter recently with a representative of the " Rochdale Times," told the reporter a graphic story of his own experience of this. Mr Ernest Pickford, the I gentleman in question, who resides at 105, Greenbank- road, Rochdale, is a well-built, broad—shouldered young , man of 22 years of ago, now in the very best of health, I though some time since his friend's feared they would 'lose him through a serious attack of typhoid fever. "My case was considered hopeless," 6aid Mr Pick- , ford " And lam fairly convinced that I sho.ld not be 1 alive now had it not been for Dr. Williams' pink pil:s for pale people. About three years ago, I had a very severe attack of enteric fever, which left me thoroughly broken down in health, and in a state of great budily weakness. I had no appetite for my food, and what I was able to eat generally came back again. I bad most violent fits of vomiting, and suffered awful pain in the bowels. For a time I was an in-patient of the Rochdale Infirmary, and it was thought that I should have to undergo an operation for a twist of the bowels caused by the vomiting fits, but happily this was not necessary, and eventually I was able to leave the Infir- mary, though I was very little better than when I entered it. I was under the best medical treatment in the town, but the vomiting fits centinued, and the slightest exertion exhausted me completely. I had seen Dr. Williams' pink pills spoken highly of in the papers, and about two months after leaving the Infirmary I decided to try them. "All my friends thought I was in a consumption, and considered there was no hope of recovery for me, but lafter taking a box of Dr. Williams' pink pills I began to feel better. Be' the time I had taken half the second box my appetite returned, and I was able to take short walks without:feeling thoroughly done up. Gradually my health improved in all directions, and after taking seven Foxes I wee a new man completely, and able to follow my employment again. In conclusion I may say that since taking the pills I have never suffered from a day's illness,"

On Wednesday afternoon the Liverpool police ra,ded two cusiness premises, one in Tithebarn -street and the other in Canning Place, aud arrested altogether about forty men and women on various charges of keeping or frequenting betting houses. They were brought before the magistrates shortly after. The great majority of the defendants were bound over to beef good behaviour, the principals being remanded untfil to-morrow.

In this transition period of the rules of procedure i seems that his suspension is indefinite: and he certainly deserves to be severely penalised for having so grossly violated not only every canon of good -inners, but the dignity and etiquette of

the House of Commons. The Government have introduced a very long and ambitious programme for the session: but the rumours on all side are of an early dissolution and a general.election before Christmas. How much foundation these have, ía is difficult at present to tell: but political activity is marked on every side.

General Viljoen, who had the reputation during late war of being such a dare-devil sort of person, has after all been the first of the Boer generals to lecture in England: and the impression he created was a most favourable one, lie had not spoken six sentences at the Queen's Hall before he had secured the sympathy of his audience : and after that he went ahead with a most racy and amusing account of various incidents, combined with a good deal of sound and unbiassed criticism. The greatest point of the whole lecture was the candid admission of the Boers' bewilderment at our abandonment of Spion Kop, just when in their estimation we had won the key to the whole posi- tion: and this statement does not reflect great credit on some of the officers concerned. Of General quller he spoke warmly. and of Lord Kitchenes

in most friendly terms. Of other generals he was more vaguely critical, but did not spare some on his own side, whom he described as better fitted to be parsons or circus clowns: but they, he quaintly noted, were soon disposed of. Of Tommy Atkins he had nothing but good to say: and he warmly praised the British, officers and men. St. Helena he' did not find so happy. General Viljoen spoke hopefully of the ultitoate settlement of South Africa and friendly relations between Boer and Briton. He was very outspoken, but never offensive.

America is at present greatly excited and much ilivided over the "poison by post" case, which may almost be considered to rank as a Yankee Tiehborne case for length and the immense interest it has called forth. On December 24th, .1898, llarry Cornish, physical director of the Knicker- bocker Club of New York, received anonymously bv post a bottle of bromo-s,ltzer in a silver stand- c•Sr- If this he toolr if, and some he gave to,

us aunt, Mrs. Adams; and, while he was oily very ill. she died of cyanide of me/vary ro;:souing,., Suspicion was thrown on Mr. Roland 13. Molineux, a New York clubman and eon of General Mohnen' ; and he was arrested on Febivary '2Bth, 1899. On February 10th, 1900, he was convicted and sentenced to electrocution at Sing-Sing: but he appealed, and on October 15th, 1901, a fresh trial was ordered. This is just now taking place and being followed with breath- less interebt. The case, whether Mohnen' is guilty or not, is a grave criticism on the state of American justice, where there is one law for the rich and another for the poor, while any case can be systematically delayed by a clever Lawyer

THE NEW STATE CARRIAGE, WHICH WILL USED FOR THE, PIRtsT TIME ON SATURDAY. of the Royal Horse Guards, which will precede the 10th and 70th batteries of Field Artillery, four or five squadrons of cavalry and another mounted band. Next will ride sixty of the King's A.D.C.'s and the Headquarters Staff, which will make about forty in all and will be flanked by the Commander-in-Chief. Then will come four pair- horsed and four four-horsed carriages, containing the members of the royal family and household: and immediately behind these a field officer's escort of the Ist Life Guards, in front of the State Carriage, drawn by the eight famous creams, beside which will ride the Prince of Wales and the Duke of Connaught just in front of the Royal Standard. Next will ride Prince Christian, the Duke of Argyll, Prince Charles of Denmark and Sir Henry Trotter: and the rear will be brought up by an escort of Life Guards. From this it will be seen that Saturday's pageant will be a most imposing spectacle. At Temple Bar the Lord Mayor, with the two senior and the two junior Aldermen, will receive their Majesties, and two civic coaches will be added to the procession to the Guildhall, where the reception before the luncheon will take place in a special pavilion built on to the entrance as an annexe. After the luncheon the procession will reform and continue its tour round the South side, as originally constituted. On Sunday the Thanksgiving Service in St. Paul's will be as far as possible open to the public by the King's special wish : but, of course, a certain number of seats will be reserved for special guests, the peers and the Commons, who will attend in Court or levee dress. This, too, promises to be a most impressive ceremony and one which will ap- peal direct to the hearts , of the people: and on Sunday the King may expect an even greater ova- tion on this great occasion for en- thusiasm and thanksgiving. On Monday the re- view of Foot MAJOR-GENERAL ARTHUR Guards, recently AGE back from South PT, Africa will take COMMANDING THE FOOT GUARDS BRIGADE. place on the Horse Guards' Parade. The vari- ous regiments will march thrr. gh the streets dur- ing the morning to the parade ground; so that many will be able to see them and welcome them home. They have done excellent service in South Africa and deserve well of the public, who are quite ready to afford them the reception they have earnt. Lord Roberts and the Headquarters' Staff will be on the Horse Guards' Parade, as well as many generals and old Guards' officers. Major-General Arthur Paget has recently been appointed to the Foot Guards Brigade of the First Army Corps; and most of the newly-returned Guards will be under his direct command. This will be a very busy sub memorable week-end.

It was prophesied that this session would be a somewhat Iturbulent one, but no one anticipated such a lively opening as took place owing to the absolutely wild cnrduct of Mr. O'Donnell, member for West Kerry. This unruly Irish Member has just undergone six months' imprisonment and has three other sentences of a month each hanging over his head: and these have not tended to soften his hostile attitude towards the Government, especially Mr. Balfour and Mr. Wyndham. In the House his grievence was that in Ireland he was imprisoned, whilst in the House of Commons he was gagged and not allowed to air his complaints. As he rose, Mr. Balfour had risen to move the closure: and Mr. O'Donnell gave vent to the most violent outburst ever seen at Westminster, raving and shouting, and ultimately rushing down the gangway towards Mr. Balfour, waving his fists. For a moment he looked as though he were going to strike the Premier, but refrained. Of what he said not a word could be
