OCLOBER 24th 1902

Two infallible 89133V1 Education Bill.—Con- cessions Begin. toms s aggoi t ato ti opnr o vaeg t;lst: the Education Bill is on the verge of succeto Lord ROM:SERI( has come out from his tent lead it, and Mr BALFOUR has begun to make c°11; cessions. Some months ago Lord RossusaY °ha' that the Bill was a very good one, if it could amended on one or two points. He now at us all to fight it "to the death." There could
_ no more encouraging evidence of the drift oc Pat' lar opinion. As for Mr. BALFOUR'S COEICoSSi°I3Sf fie they are, we fear, more apparent than real. rbe

will not alter the proportions which give LPO-1 Church a majority of two to one on boards management of the Volunt6y Schools, but 10 wishes us to believe that while these irresponsib gentlemen are called " managers the real " °Sr

trol " is to rest with the —County or Boror Council. This is a subtle but wii‘i new distinction. In July Mr. BILFOv3 s' that it wou.al be " monstrously and 'Ate unjust" to grant "what was called 1301 lar control and management of donor national schools." Clearly he had not then Int this distinction between control and managerne and he was equally opposed to the idea of one'

ing either. If ho proposes to alter the 13 ill at it will be in the direction of strengthening tig hands of the County Council, which is app ireet:e to have some control over the expenditure of t"3, money which it raises. But it is small comPel3.9i, tion to learn that the public will have the Pr1:110 loge of paying the salaries of the teachers 0,1-0 the Church continues to appoint them. This 15,1 worthless ccncession, even if the whole busineSs f financing the schools is taken out of the hancish°o the local boards. The status of the teachers is real crux of the educational problem. So 104 they are chosen by the Church trustees, 3130 subjected to theological tests, their case will 1019 hard as it was when the denominational scilc)°,f were really voluntary. The whole scandal English education is at bottom a teachers' (111e3,4 tion. In the clerical schools at present °DIY , per cent, of teachers hold certificates of e°l3l petency, and of these scarcely half have evel attended a training-college, whereas in Scotai° , most of the male teachers of the younger gerlert; tion have had a University education. s()C3 certificated teacher has to wrestle with children, The average salary of a woman, al's; she be head-mistress, is only £5B, and if a 1113 f (not a head-maste'r) £B3. To alter this stato°'; things is to solve the educational problem. 111 first step is to emancipate the teacher from the Church,

As TRANOE and unwonted The Decay of spirit of enterprise on the Billingsgate. part of the Corporation of London threatens—so it :seems—one of the oldest and most famous institutions in theland. Common, Councillors are pressing for the removal of the great and, shall we say, " historic " fish market of Billingsgate, which has created an atmosphere, a flavour, and a language of its own. The idea is to develop a thoroughly conventional and modern market at Shadwell, and to sacrifice the magnifi- cent rents which are paid for the reputation, from the traders' point of view, of having Billingsgate for an address. To them the name has been what Covent Garden is to the florist, Mincing-lane to the tea merchant, and the Burlington Arcade to the hosier. It gives what is called in the London vernacular "cl ass." Still, however, dissatisfaction exists. . .

But Billingsgate has a more remote claim to our interest than that. According to Sir WALTER BESANT, in his charming book "East L mdon,' the first London bridge—the Roman bridge, built of wood—had its north end hard by. He has given us a curious picture of what the port was like in Roman times; with half-a-do en merchantmen lying moored to the w@oden quays; upon them bales of wood, bundles of skins, bars of iron, wait- ing to be taken on board; rolls of cloth and of silk imported; boxes containing weapons, casks of wine taken out of ships and waiting ,to be carried up into the citadel ; in one corner a little group of British women and children going over to slavery in some distant part of the Roman Empire. We may shift the scene forward a little, and contemplate the English going to Rome from the same port, and the aged POPE remarking of those young men from Billingsgate: "They are not English; they are Angels." The phrase is familiar. Then we come to the claim of ELIA. CHARLES Lams, in that sonnet to "The Female Orators," urges that the very name is strictly allu- sive to two tongues: Her school hard by, the Goddess Rhethoric Opes. And gratis deals to 0s ter Wives her tropes. With Nereid Green, Green Nereid disputes. Replies, rej Ana, confutes and still confutes Hence Pulpits rail ; Grave Senates learn to jar ; Quacks scold ; and Billingsgate infdcts the Bar. All this is past. The fishwoman has bee banished from the place; she lingers still in the dried fish market, but her tongue had lost its old cunning and melifluousness ; and whatever happens to Billingsgate nobody is concerned for it as a school of rhetoric. It is in regard to the practical consideration of the prosperity of the fishermen, the fish-factors, and the interests of the consumers that its Pate has to be determined. The experiments made by a big company and a private firm at Shadwell failed,and it should be possible to enlarge Billing,sgate by pulling down houses and opening up space for traffic. The harvest of the sea is not yielding in- come in the same easy way that it did, and it is necessary for those concerned in the trade to go warily and cautiously. The question is too large to discuss at length here ; but our English trawlers, who now have to go further for their hauls and have to meet such limn competition, should watch carefully any proposals which may affect their markets, and determine their weight of influence accordingly. A change of venue , brings a change in the position of buyers, and turns events in many ways. No definite motion has yet been made for the transfer of the market, and iG is certain that, although a number of people a.re quietly working For a change, the matter will be most seriously deliberated before anything is I done. The Court of Common Council is a sedate body ; and it may even come to pass that we shall hear Billingsgate at the bar of the House of Commons.

-- Among all our prominent politicians there is no student of public opinion who can rival Lord Rose- bery. He has the instinct that discerns the flow- ing tide, and he moves with it as naturally as the sunflower follows the sun. If anyone doubted that the agitation against the Education Bill is on the road to success he must have been reassured to find Lord Rosebery its partner. For note the history of his lordship's public opinions on this subject. His earliest utterance wholly blessed the Bill, because it would add dignity to municipal life. Even after the Leeds election he said that it was a very good Bill indeed if it could be amended in one or two points. But now he has made a tremendous ovation against it at the City Liberal Club. His language was almost incoherent in his violence, and the gist of all his remarks was that there can be no compromise at all. This "very good Bill," with the two or three blemishes which would have added so much to "the dignity of municipal life," must be "fought to the death." But somehow, for all his readiness to come into line with extreme Radicalism on this point, Lord Rosebery is not a whit more willing to co-operate with Sir Henry Campbell-Banner- man. He will do so, he tells Mr. Black in a series of published letters, if only Sir Henry will cease to oppose the Chesterfield policy. The " clean slate," one hopes, is no more likely to become a Liberal emblem than the well-oiled weather-cock to which it bears so odd a resemblance.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EAR LES TOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EAR LES TOWN.

1.13 Y A CORRESPONDEN Tl. FOOTBALL. Earlestown had a blank Jay on Saturday last and perhaps it was as well that they had in view of the stiff enconnter they have on hand to-morrow (Saturday) when Southport Central visit the e Mesnes. It is to be hoped that Earlestown give a different exhibition to the one they gave at :Southport a fortnight ago Several new faces will again be seen in the team. Brown,late of St llelens Town,will figure at centre,whilst negotiations have been proceeding for the transfer of lienry,the clever little inside left from Presoot. If his signature is obtained, he should prove a decided acquisition to an otherwise weak forward line.

NeWton received another drubbing at the hands of Witton Albion@ on Saturday, altijoußli they were not expected to bring points from the Cheshire club's enclosure. Although at the interval the score stood at one each, Witton had all the play during the second moiety and ran out winners by five goals to two.

The lot of a referee in the Warrington ' league does not seem to be a very happy one, at any rate ti the experience of Mr Forbes in the Buttonwood v. Latchford Brit- annia match playea at Buttonwood on Saturday, is to be taken as an example. The game resulted in a draw, no goals being scored, and this state of affairs evidently did nbt suit the Buttonwood spectators. Several of Mr Forbes's decisions had been particularly unpalatable to the crowd, but they did not take up an objectionable attitude until a Burtonwood player was ordered off the field tor kicking an opponent. This was the signal for a regular fusilade of nasty remarks, personal and otherwise, directed at the unfortunate official, who had to threaten to stop the game, before the shout- ing subsided. When the final whistle blew it looked very much as if Mr Forbes was in for a rough handling by a certain section of the crowd, but they eventually thought better of it, and con- tented thera.-elves by hurling harmless remarks at the official, from a safe distance lam afraid that • the greater number of these self same spectators would present a sorry spectacle were they to be lace d in charce of a match similar to the one nder notice, although they are evidently puffed p wi t h their knowledge of the rules of the game, om the way in which they were kind enough to vi se Mr Forbes on Saturday.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY.

The monthly meeting of the Free Library com- mittee was held on Tuesday, Mr Hope in the chair: —The librarian Mrs Jones, reported that the num- ber of issues was 2.409; daily average, 109; number of days open, 22. Details of issues—lending depart- ment, theology, 20; philosophy, 8; science, 84; history, Stc., 123; poetry, 10; fiction, 1848; mis- cellaneous, 194; French literature, 7; music, 10; total, 2,304; reference department, 105. The totai increase on the corresponding mouth of last year was 703. The chairman said that it was common knowledge that they had sent an application to Mr Carnegie at the last meetiog but no reply had yet been received. CHARGE AGAINST A PUBLICAN.

At Widn-es,on Thursday, William Henry ihoraton landlord of the Queen's Arms, Warrington-road,was charged with an assault on Mrs Harriet Burns on Saturday night, Mr Riley appeared for Burns, and Mr Knowles for defendant—from the evidence it appeared that Mrs Burns went at half-past ten for some supper been& row had been going on previous to Mrs Burns entering and she was in conversation with one of the men who had taken part in the row. Thornton it is alleged, was annoyed at the woman talking to the man,whereupon he was stated to have poured her beer away and struck her a violent blow on the shoulder.—Several witnesses were called in support,but the facts were denied by Mr Knowles. The case was dismissed. SHOCKING NEGLECT OF CHILDREN AT WIDNES. Before Mr H Wade Deacon and Mr T S fimmis, at Widnes on Thursday, John Riley and Ann Goff, living in Sankey-street, Widnes, were each sent to gaol for three months for neglecting twin children on different dates daring the last six months, The male prisoner was also sent to gaol for a month on each of two charges of drunkenness, and one month for a breach of the peace on the 12th and 13th inst. The police evidence revealed a shocking state 01 home affairs. Clothing was conspicuous by its absence, and the only utensils at band were two tin cups. The rooms, both upstairs and down,were filthy, and had never been cleaned for over a week Drink and laziness were the causes of this desola- tion.—Dr llutchinson,who gave evidence on behalf of the _National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, said that the house was unfit for human habitation, and that the surroundings in particular would cause injury to health.

div.head: WIDNES WWI' It-N'S TIIEFT:
div.p: A WIDNES WWI' It-N'S TIIEFT:

At Widnes' on Monday, Eliza Molyneux, 54, Birchfield-road, was charged with stealing from the dwelling-house of Mrs Price, Birchfield-road, on dates between July and the present month, three tablecloths, six table forks, six teaspoons, one cruet spoon, one table knife, six dessert spoons, one print blouse, three pairs of boots, and one pair of stock- ings, value XL—Mary Price, widow, said she em- ployed defendant several days a week to do some cleaning, On the 10th of the present month she placed a pair of boots on the landing, and going up a short time after, she found they had gone. Sus- picion fell on Mrs Molyneux, and she was at once seen about the matter, but she stated that she had not seen the boots. Shortly afterwards defendant sent the boots back to Mrs Price, saying that she had taken them in mistake.lnformation was given to the police,and the remainder of the articles were trac- ed to be in her possession—Mr Joseph Stout,assist- ant pawnbroker to Mr G J Neil, gave evidence of the pawning of several articles on different dates. Police-constable Turner also gave details of arrest and the finding of the remainder of the articles at her house.—The Mayor, after administering a cau- tion, imposed a fine of 10i and costs, or fourteen days. THEFT FROM A FATHER'S HOUSE.

At the RUEICOM Police Court on Saturday, before Mr E Imison (in the chair) and Mr S Taylor, Edward Roylauce Gatley (10) was charged with, having burglariously broken and entered the shop of John Gatley, 25, Church-street, Runcorn, some- time between 10.30 p m on the 15th inst. and 2 a m on the IGth. and stolen a silver watch and chain the property of James Woodward.—Subsequently the charge was reduced to one of theft only—Evidence proving the case was called Defendant pleaded guilty, and elected to be deali, With summarily.—Mr Woodward asked the magis- trates to deal as leniently as possible with him.—ln answer to the magistrates, Mr Gatley said his son had been a steady youth. He had worked for Iseveral years for a firm in Runcorn, and he had nothing to say against him. He had bean at Man- chester six or seven weeks.—The Chairman said that defendant would be fined .El, or in default of payment would have to go to gaol for 14 days. The magistrates had taken a very lenient view of the case. Defendant had acted very improperly. If he continued to carry on in this way he had a very dark future before him.

div.head: SERIOUS ASSAULT BY A SA!LOR
div.p: SERIOUS ASSAULT BY A SA!LOR

At the Runcorn Police Court on Tuesday before Messrs F J Norman and J Ockleston, a sailor named Edward Nieksoo, of Amlwela was charged with assaulting William Coe, of Palmoutb, captain of the schooner Gem, of Gloucester. Captain Coe stated that prisoner had sailed with him for three Inonths. On the 4th Ootober at Poole, the prisoner came aboard tho wo-ss for drink and insulted him' He forgave the prisoner. On the passage frcm P.mle to Runcorn with acargo of pipe clay the prisoner threatened to throw him overboard and on reaching port on Monday he gave prisoner notice to quit the ship and then went ashore. When he re- turned at 11 p.m. the prisoner demanded a reason why he had been ordered to leave and he replied that he had nothing to say to him. The prisoner there- upon struck him twice on the face with his fist, and WS wife coming between them be also struck her. He then gave him in charge of the canal constable and on the and toc thee d phoim n h !icoti sttate face bruising herpursionner knocked him down d kk his cheek and black- ing his eye.— the constable did not see the assault on the ship and Mr Norman informed the prisoner he bad been illegally arrested and discharged him. The criaoner, however, was at once re-arrested on a warrant taken out by the captain.—Thomas Leach and Henry Moores, canal constables, testified to the assault on I shore, an the prifoner was fined 403 and costs lls 61 or a month.—The money was paid.— 'There Was a further charge against Nickson of assault leg Moores, and a charge agair,st another sailor named Robert Williams, of Port Madre, of obstructing Leach, but on the advice of the magistrates these charges were withdrawn. The magistrates informed the canal con- stable they had no right to arrest these rsi.n under the circumstances without a warrant, and Mr Norman sug- gested that they should confer with Superintendent EDl:lien as to the extent of their powers. RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the members of the Runcorn Rural District Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday. There were present : Messrs J Knowles (chairman), E Clarke, J:Mclntyre, J Stokes, r Darlington, C E Linaker, J T Lewis, W H Bradford, T Wright, F T Collier, 9 Woodward, G Pilling, S Norton, E Bretherton, J Nickson, J Spruce, A P Jones-Parry, J Mount, A G Guest, T Antwis, with Mnssrs G F Ashton (clerk), WE Hough (assistant clerk), Dr Adams (medical officer), W Farrington (inspector), W Diggle and J Swinton (surveyors).

div.head: CLOSING OF A FOOTPATH.
div.p: THE CLOSING OF A FOOTPATH.

Mr J Longland, solicitor, Warrington,wrote enclosing an application from Mr C IN Davenport for the consent of the Council to the stepping of a footpath beGween Michell-street and Farreli-screet at S7.ock:on Heath and forwarding a tracing of plan showing the locality. Mr Longland made a personal application to support the closing of the footpath. He explained that the footpath was the remains oi an old one that used to run into the south side of London Bridge. It crcsied the fields and came one on the green by Whitefield-road. The greater part of it had already bei n absorlrd in the new streets which had been made. All that remained of the road was 120 yards and until permission was granted the land would not be available for building purposes. The ratable value would be increased by its closing. It was really of no advantage to the public who would not be hindered in any way by the closing of the path. There was no local obj c:ion. Resolved, after further discussion, that ars applica- tion be granted.

div.head: POLLUTION OF LOCAL BROOK.
div.p: THE POLLUTION OF LOCAL BROOK.

The Clerk of the County Council wrote on Octobr Rh intimating that the Rivers P Alution Committee would meet oa the 24th and asking what stop; the Coun- cil had taken upon his letter of August 7th to stop the pollution of Kingsley Brook. The Clerk explained that co far as El ;kb? was con- cerned the work was already lo,ing done by carriTing out a sewage scheme. The Halton Council and th 3 Parochial Committee were also considering a scheme and the Clerk had received instructions to apply to the landowners for the and he required for purification works. A letter had been received from the Kingsley Parish Council. Mr. Woodward chairman of the Kingsley Parish Council would probably have something to say respecting the question. Mr Wo olward said that he had found certain propor- ties were contributing sewage to the brook, and this had now been stopped. There were several others still putting sewage into the brook and he sugg,estod that the Medical Officer and the Nuisance Inspector meet the committee of the Parish Counci who had the matter in hand and that the owner of the properties be nttifiad of the proposed aionsultation. Passed after considerable discussion.

Mr Woodward further proposed thit the Surveyor also clean out the brook as the stones would m.ore than c pensate for the labour. After considerable discussion this was agreed to. Mr Linaker said he would give notice that he would aqk the time taken to clean the bro and whether the stones compensated tor the labour.

Mr Reginald Potts, clerk to the Ch 'shire C niticy Council, wrote asking whether the D,strict C3oncil had any objection to an application of the National Telephone Company to erect poles aloog the main road from Quarry-lane to Strelton about 85 yards apart. On the same subject, the surveyor, Mr J Swinton, wrote that the proposal would greatly obstruct the foot- paths on the road which were nerrow, there being tele- graph poles on the other side of the road. Resolvid that the Council do not object to the erection of the poles, but suggest that the poles be painted white for a certain length from the ground.

div.head: TIIELWALL NUISANCE,
div.p: TIIELWALL NUISANCE,

Mr Reginald Potts, clerk to the Cheshire County Council, seat the following letter to the Rural District Council, which was to be read when the Pale!ic Health Committee of the County Council met, The letter emanated from Mr W B Coek, clerk to the rhelwall Parish Council, stating that they were not satisfied with the dilatory way in which the Rural District Council had dealt with the nuisance itt Woaste-latte, obi tcciu to he saddled with an expensive sewage scheme until the origin of the nuisance had been ascertained, and asking that a special inquiry be held to inquire into the origin of the nuisance.

_ Mr Pilling said the C)rmnittee appointed to inquire into the Tnelwall uMsance had met that morning, and as a result recommended that the engineer prepare a sewage scheme tor Thelwall, and that Weaste-lane be proceeded with at once. Admiral Jones-Parry objected, in a lengthy speech, to the saddling of an exponsiv, sewage schnme on Thlll until the decision of the County Council had been heard on the matter. After a long discussion, many resolutions and more amendments, it was resolved that the Coancil take no action in the proposed sewage soheme until they load heard the decision of the County Council.

div.head: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON
div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON
ALLEGED THEFT BY AN EARLESTOWN MAN.

At the Newton Police Court on Monday, James Burh, of the Vulcan, Earlestown, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at Winwick On Saturday afternoon, and also with stealing a glass jug and a glass tumbler, of the value of 91, the property of James Schofield Barlow, landlord of the Swan Hotel, Winwick. It appears that the prisoner was found drunk by P.C. Woof, and when proceed- ing to the Police Station the articles named were found in his possessioq. The defendant was fined 2s Gd for the drunkenness, whilst the charge of theft was remanded for a fortnight. ST. Joimis CHURCH EXTENSION. The second Pierrot concert of the series promoted in aid of the propo,ed extension of St John's Church Earlestown, took place in the Town Hall on Thurs- day evening. There was a vary fair audience who thoroughly enjoyed the various items submitted for the delectation. The artifices were Messrs Noah Johnson (baritone), Fred Morgan (Professor of Elo- cution), solo banjoist and vocalist, J E Sykes ; Miss L Skeet ( soprano), Miss Emille Marsland (contralto), and Mr James Foye (tenor). All the items in a well-chosen programme were capitally submitted, the recitations by Mr Fred Morgan being especially worthy of mention, his portraitures being most life-like. EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN CHTYRCH.

On Thursday night, the Rev r rank E iward.s, the Chaplain of the South Wales Borderers, and who accompanied this Regiment in their recent Sout h African campaign. delivered to a capital audience at the above church, a lecture entitled " Up with the fighting line." Mr Mitchell, of St iielens,occu- pied the chair,and after the opening hymn had been sung, the Secretary of the District Branch of the Wesleyan Foteign Missionary Society read his annual report. The Rev Frank Edwards commenc- ed his lecture by explaining his reasons for acccm- panying the South Wales Borderers to South Africa. tie noticed that although there were several Welsh Regiments going cut to South Africa there were no Welsh chaplains, and knowing how dear to the Walsh s)ldier is his own native tongue, he decided to volunteer as a chaplain He was sure they would agree with him that this war had proved the dauntless courage, and bull- dog tenacity of the British soldier as it had never been proved since the days of the Spanish Armado. Describing a meeting with a company of the Grenadier Guards after the latter had returned from a long and tiring march, the speaker said that when he looked at that lot of scarecrows sat round the room, he could hardly realize that these soldiers consisted of the cream of the British aristocracy, they looked more like tramps than anything else. One of the most terrible things they had to put up with was thirst. He had seen " the lads " rush like dogs the moment they came upon water notwithstanding the fact that this water was oftener than not, unfit to wash in. This was the chief cause of that terrible scourge enteric. After vividly describing his experience of the Zard River fight the lecturer went on to explain the effect the playing of the reginacntal march "The Men of Har- lech" had, on a Regiment, completly done up after a long and tiring march to Kroonstad, rousing them from what resembled a band of old men.marching,to a smart British Regiment.

div.head: RUNCORN TECHNICAL INST 11 UTE. Annual Distribution of Prizes.
div.p: RUNCORN TECHNICAL INST 11 UTE. Annual Distribution of Prizes.
Sir E. Russell on Education.

The annual distribution of priz.s in connection with the Technical Institute evening classes and day school took plata, in tae school room on Wednesday evening. There was a large ateeddance of parents and scholars. Mr S Taylor, occupied the chair and he wail supported by Sir Ed ward Russell, :desire E Irnison, F Beck, F J Norman, W Headley. W Wilding, F Hatton, J Turnbull, G Bellamy, S Pope, J R Frith, J M Frith, A R Norman, E Marshall (secretary), Lawrenson (headmaster), E Wilsen, R H Posnett, Rev H B Firth, M.A., J Osborne, M.d, and others. Mr Marshsil read a letter from Canon Wood apologia- log for his absence on the ground that he had to address a meeting out of town. The Cnairmau said tney were delighted to have Sir E Russell with them that evening. It was well kaowa that he had many engagements to fulfil and he (Mr raylor) was never more pleased than when lee learned they had secured him to distribute the prizes. He was a great educationalist and had taken a great deal of interest in educational matter. He was a distinguished writer and had to a great extent led the country in education concerns. Runcorn was not a large town but its citizens nevertheless were education- alists. He was safe in saying that for its size Runcorn could not be surpassed in the country, considering its science and evening classes. They had 20 evening classes with 400 on the register and 314 scholars. The beer and spirit tax was a blessing to Cheshire The County Council had £17,000 through the tax at their disposal with no restriction save that it had to be used for education. They decided they would use the whole of the fund and wonid help all those bodies wile helped themselves. Accordingly Runcorn decided to take Id in the £ out ot the rates, and they got an equal sum train th 3 Council. They thus got their splendid Techni- cal Destitute which was equal, if not superior, to any of in size. It was doing a grand work, whica was as yet in its infancy. They had uphill work to commence' with but now the working class saw it was meant for their benefit and were trying to appreciate their work. The fact that Sir Edward had to distribute 60 or 70 prizes was sufficient to demonstrate the value and the exten- siveness of the work toeing carried on. The headmaster (Mr I. evereeson) in the course of his report said that last Chliatmas two pupils were entered for the Cambridge local examination held at Widnes,and of these L Stubbs gained third class honours in the senior, and Etuel Lunt passed in the junior. In June 1902, G Robinson, Eli .1 Lunt and Leon S:ubbs passed ..second class in the seceud stage mathematics. In July the Oxford local exeminttion was held in the school, Runcorn having been made the local centre for this examination for the firet time. The successes included George Robinson, who gained third class honours in the senior examination. Ethel Lunt, R Newport,Percy Hill and G Warburton, who passed in the junior. In the preliminary E'sie Grice, Burns, Baxter, Ellieon, Gough, Haliday, Hardman, Kulcross, and Robinson passed. The past year had several features of interest. They had established four local science and art scOolarships of considerable value by the assistance of the Board of Education ad c intribu- :ions from various sources. Toey had been able by the help of the Council to rent a field for boys and girls, and oricket and football clubs for the boys, and tennis and hockey clubs for the girls lead been formed. The first athletic sports in July proved very successful. The girls had also held a debating Society, and wound up the term with a picnic to Hetsby. A dynamo and gas engine had been put down, which together with the new honours board in the main corridor marked the main additions to the equipment of the Institute. Their car- rioutum was stilt that of a Government secondary sehool. Division A. This provided a thorough and progressive course in science together with the subjects of a general education. He dealt with the teaching in detail, and in conclusion re- ferred to the career of several former pupils. Sir Edward Russell who was received with applause, said they had been goad enough to speak in terms of great kindness. He really owed a debt of gratitude to the Chairman for asking him to come to Runcorn. It was a source of satisfaction that they in Runcorn were such true educationalists. He meant by that that the working people of Runcorn had come to believe in edu- cation and had availed themselves of it. The trust had I been reposed with the people and they had nobly res- ponded to it. The appeal of patriotism never went I without response. Bt in the matter of education there I had been a lamentable backwardness. A great number of children who could earn money were sent out to earn it as soon as they possibly could. There was nothing more fatal to the Society than such a I practice except absolute sq.daled idleness. It was the worst curse that could come upon a people to take away children at an untimely age from educational pursuits, which, if foil wed out, would enable them to fight the battle of life. Such pursuits I would bring happiness into their lives and give them immeasurable advantages which would make them superior to those who had been forced to go early to work. He wished to say samething to encourage the young in the devotion to their work. There had to be reakenthusiasm in the pursuit of knowledge. The busi- ness of youth was to acquire skill in the work of the I mind and the hands. They knew that education at the I Present time was in the air, and it was making things I rather warm. But, he thought, they had the advantage of knowing that ore the platform of secondary education they all could meet without differences. These secondary studies wouldirevolutionise the methods of the country. They could see the necessity of education and know— ledge. If they did not mean to be passed in the race they would have to alter their system of education. He was confident that the matter had at last got hold of the nation. All the local holies were rivalling each cther in the introducing and carrying out of changes for the betterment of education. They had scholar- ships Government grants, &a, all ef which were signs of the times. The curriculu:n now covered a vast amount of practical education. It lead been a curse to secondary schools that they had in many cases to give the child first an elementary education. It was a disgrace that the country should be behind other countries in the matter of elementary educ ttion. The studies of the school were all necessary to the life of the n etion. It would be well, however, for the rounding of the character if they made literature a portion of their work. Nothing would add more to the pleasure and utility of life than a study of the best writings. They could not be the worse for being educated, but must necessarily be the better for it. It gave a care -r of intellectual enjoyment to everyone who pursued it. It could not stop with the school, but had to be carried on se that when they grew to manhood they could converse reason- ably and sensibly on any topic. They would all have to admit they had been too much addicted to the hand-to- mouth training. But, as in other c ises, they ;always come out right. They could not, however, depend on the saying of Mr Balfour that the shop was the place to learn to do the work and not the school. The school should always be put first and science should always be used as an instrument to education which should be caeried into daily practice in their liveß. He for one looked forward to general education fur the great progress of the country in the future. They should realize la ow deen'y the interests of the country were in- volved in it. Education never degraded a being, but or the contrary produced high thought and added an additional dignity to life. When communities like Run- corn realized such facts and bronght their, children up in such a knowledge then such a state of happiness would be reached as it Was impossible to describe. , (Applause). Sir Edward Russell then delivered the prizes and the I certificates to the successful students. After which I Mr Wilson, chairman of the Technical Commiteee, I proposed a vote of thanks to Sir Edward Rue sell for hie splendid address. His work, he said, brought him in : direct touch with the citizens of the town and be was pie' s,d to say that their work since the erection of the Institute had mafetielly improved. (Applause.) Mr Elandl-y seconded, remarking that Sir Edward Russell was an exemplification of literary ability. The proposition was unanimously carried. Sir Edward in returning thanks proposed a similar honour to the Chairman which was carried with ap- plause, on the motion of Messrs R H P.ienett and Lawrence.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES. – Lay A CORRESP3NDENT.]
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES. - Lay A CORRESP3NDENT.]

The Beard of Guardians had very little bu&iness to trans.an at their meeting on Tuesday. The usual quarterly vaccination fees gave rise to the usual murmurs of astonishment. The Beard evidently wish that the old order of things had not given place to new. Of course the Board have no option but to "pay ! pay ! pay !" And they hand the money over with much the same grace that some unlucky traveller does when asked to disgorge by an armed highwayman.

--- Apropos of vaccination there was, by the way, likely to nave been a scene at the Police Court on Monday. The Rev J Osborne, M.A., applied before the magistrates—Messrs J Ockleston and W Tim- mins—for the usual certificate exempting his twin children from being vaccinated on the ground that he had a conscientious objection. The Chairman then asked the applicant to state the grounds of his conscientious objection Accordingly Mr Osborde stated his views at length and adduced reasons sufficient to prove to any impartial person that his objection was the result of conviction, Nevertheless it was easy to see that Mr Ockleston was by no means satisfied that the objection was a conscientious one. And a consider sole time elapsed—in consultation with the magis- trates clerk, Mr Frank Johnson—before the application was granted. Mr Ockleston was then understood to say that the bench considered Mr Osborne was acting very foolishly and that if any- thing untoward happened to the children he would certainly be to blame. Of course it is all very well for the magistrates to deliver well-meant homilies to persons—sometimes better qualified to form an opinion on the merits of a case than tee magistrates themselves—but such addresses are altogether un- necessary and are not sanctioned by law. The majority of magistrates forget entirely teat the merelfact of a man:being willing to lose his time and his money to procure a certificate is in itself an objection which must be based on "conscientious- ness." Further the magistrates by the act have only to be convinced that the applicant has a " con- scientious objection." And all that the magistrate has to do is to hear th a applicant formally state the fact. It is no business of the bench at all to inquire into the grounds of the objection. This point wag proved at a London Court the other day before a stipendary when the applicant declined to state his grounds and merely contented himself with the phrase "I hate a conscientious objection." Perhaps by the time the law respecting the con- scientious objector expires magistrates will have learned precisely and specifically their limitations and their privileges.

The pollution of the public brooks is a question still engaging the attention of the County Council and the Parish Councils of Halton, Kingsley and Helsby. It is interesting to know that in Halton and Helsby steps are being taken which will land the villages in a more or less costly sewage scheme The Kingsley authority has contented itself with stopping certain occupants from turning sewage matter into Kingsley Brook and with warning others to desist from their malpractices. On the proposition of Mr Woodward—who has been dis- cribed by one well qualified to judge,as the tliink- jug man of the Council—the streamis to be cleared by the Surveyor. It was argued by Mr bunker, that the expense would fall on the District Council where it ought really to be borne by the Parish Council. Mr Woodward aQsured hia critical friend however that enough stones would be taken from the brook to more than cove; the expense. This reportapparently silenced Mr Linaker, but after a few minutes silence, as though struck by a brilliant thought, he announced his intention at a future date of inquiring into the cost of the work ; the time taken in the purifying of the Brook; and whether the remuneration was sufficient to pay for the cost. Nevertheless Mr. Woodward, by his strategy, gained his point for the betterment of his particular parish.

It is interesting to chronicle the fact that an appliCation from the Free Public Library Commit- tee has been sent to Mr. Carnegie presumably for a grant. No reply has yet been received, though the letter was despatched almost a month ago. Mean- while the Committee, thinking of the adage that " no news is good news" is eagerly waiting for an answer, buoyed up by a lively hope of success.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

In every respect it was a grand game that was witnessed at 'mall-lane on Saturday when the "Lions" and the" Linnets " embraced in deadly conflict. Runcorn were severely handicapped by the absence of Jolly and played in his place an A team half back, Forster by name. Swinton were fully represented and it was generously rece.gnised that if Runcorn meant to win they would have to put in all they knew. Neither club having been beaten this season more than usual interest centred in the encounter and there were fully four thous- and people lining the field when the vieitors started. From the outset it was seen that the visitors intended to force the game. Over and over again the front pushers heeled ont the ball:and set the rear rank in motion with a series of beautiful combined runs that, would have simply paralysed the major- ity of their teams. Luckily the home contingent were in their best defensive mood. Repeatedly Swinton $ swooped down on the line and but for the herculean efforts of Houghton , and his partners in the rear division a score must have been registered. Really the only , occasions that Runcorn made their presence felt ' were the times that a score resulted from their efforts. On each occasion they broke away grandly and baffled their opponents with the rapidity win which they changed from defensive to offensive tactics. The latter portion of the game consisted in one prolonge I furious fusilade on the home defence Several times it seemed as though the citadel must "Ic captured. But though there were several narrow shaves Runcorn can proudly boast that the lines were not even crossed. It is sufficient to say tleat • Houghton played a safe game ; that the three- quarter line did remarkably well but that Moran should have made more of his chances; that For.“er played a good game ; that the front rank were outplayed though the blame cannot directly lie at their door ; that Swinton were beaten on their merits, that the large score was not due to Swinton's poor play or Runcorn's good luck ; that they attacked like men but found an impregnable defence ; that Runcorn on the day's form, is the , first club in the Northern Union.

div.head: EARLESTOWN YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.
div.p: EARLESTOWN YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.

On Monday evening the new premises acquired by the committee who have been fostering for some months the cause of the Young Men's Christian Association in Earlestown, were opened by Colonel It Pilkington, the member for the New- ton Division, and ..the Presithlnt of the Earlestown branch.

Atter a brief ceremony at the Fairclougb-street premises of the association, the company adjourned to the Town Hall, Earlestown, where a highly suc- cessful and ,enthusiastic meeting was held. Colonel Pilklngton eccupied the chair and was aupported on the platform by the Van Archdeacon Madden, Rev T tc, Matthews, Messrs T Molyneux,A K Yapp, W B Wakefield,o Carey,and others,whilst letters of apology were reed from several gentlemen. Alter the Secretary had read a rather lengthy but in- teresting report, Colonel Pilkington said that first of all he haa to thank them for having done him the honour Of making him President ot the bugler,. He was sure the YMCA would prove to be a great benefit to the inhabitants of Earlestown. Per- haps they did not know that the age of this movement was now approaching 60 years. It was begun in the year 1844, when it began as these things always did,in a very small way. One meet- ing of 12 started this movement. There were now 8,000 centres of the Y.M.C.A., and they had 600,000 members. It had centres in practically all the great English towns in the British Colonies and in almost every Europ:An country. Tne was a resting place for anybody, any Christian man, whether he be young or old, there was no limitation of age. It was a place where a lonely man might receive help and sympathy, and would act as a safeguard against the numerous temptations which assailed young men leaving their families. It was of the utmost value to the lives of the young men who were leaving home for strange places. With regard to the question of help and encouragement and sympathy, the speaker said that they all knew that there were times in the lives of all young men, when they felt very low-spirited and very mucu discouraged, That was the time when tne Y.M.C.A. was useful. Men like himself (the speaker), who had lived 50 or 60 years, had had many temptaticiasto fight, but what must be the temptations, that young men leaving their homes and families to seek work, had to lace. Tao Y.M.C.A. was a great encouragmeut to this young man, and he could easily see in his heart of hearts that this was an institution which would bold out a helping hand to him. This move- ment in Earlestown deserved to be a gigantic suc- cess and he hoped they would receive the same amount of support as had been accorded the St Helens branch. (Applause). Archdeacon Madden, who is an enthusiast on any work relative to a Y.M.C.A. addressing the meeting after a glee had been sung by the Mazawattee Glee Party, the venerable Archdeacon said that if the Y.M.C.A. was not a success in Earlestown it would not ne the fault of the president,. It had been said that what was wanted in the Britiso Army was good officers. This was a libel, but there was no lack of good officers in the Y.M.C.A., what they wanted was the rank and file to get settled and there would be no Spion Kop's or Colenso's They had got their building, were they going to keep it going? Were they going to pay their sub- scriptions ? Of courte they were silent when he asked this. They did not cheer. On a half-hearted cheer coming from the aud- ience, the speaker sarcastically announced that "That was not very enthusiastic." rho speaker then went on to say that the object of a Y.M.O A was net to interfere with any other work that Was going on but to supplement that work. If it inter- fered, it was going out of its p!ovince. They should seek to further the work of G3d in every church or chapel with which they may be connected. There was room in Earlessown for special work of any kind. The work of a Y.M.C.A had to do with the physical,spiritual,and mental iLinds. Some of the young men or to-day wanted moral muscle. Ile wanted them to have all kinds of muscle. He had no doubt many of the young mai present lived in lodgings. If there was orie man he sympathised witn it was the young man in lodging. He was ' lonely and the public houses or the club presented a very inviting picture to his mind. The T.M.C.A. was a place where they could talk over things, where they could discuss various topics. It was all very well (or Colonel Pilkington to go to the House of Commons. They ruled the British Army ! in Earlestown. They could settle the Transvaal and South African queston and put Mr Chamberlain to , shame. The Y. NI.C.A. was not an association of mamby-pamby sort of fellows.but fellows who were ' able to walk upright in the world. (Applause.) _ _

Oa the motion of Mr T Parr,a vote )E't.hantri .wai accorded: to Colonel Pilkington, M.P., Archdeacon Madden, Messrs Yapp and Wakefield, and all who had assisted in the launching of the Y.M.C.A., and this brought the meeting to a close, da. NEWTCN-LE-WILLOWS CRICKET AND BOWLING CLUB.

The annual bowling handicap in connection with the above club, which has been in progress during the past three week ends was brought to a close on Saturday afternoon. Being oven to all the mem- bers of the club, there was consequently a numer- ous entry, and many rounds had to be played before a result was arrived at. In the end Mr Boardman was declared winner of the firs: prize,a clock given by Mr Colonel Wood; 2nd prize,ls3 by W H Davies; 3rd, R Galloway; 4th, D Davies; sth, C Appleton; 6th, T Williams ; every player receiving a prize ot some value or other. At the close of play the members adjourned to the Pied Bull hotel where an excellent dinner was provided and partaken of. Mr H J Longton presided in the absence of the Presi- dent, Mr R Stone, P., who wired from Scotland expressing his regret at being unable to be preeeut, and stating how pleased he was that his special prize had been won by Mr H Sweetlove. The Chair- man also referred to the ab,ence of the Hon Treas. Mr W H Ilindley, owing to the s,ri•Ais illness of his wife and was sure every one joined in hoping that Mrs 'Lindley would soon be restored to health. (Hear, hear). The usual loyal toasts were then proposed and duly honoured, and the chairman testified briefly to lois pleasure at seeing 80 many present and congratulated the club, of which he had the honour to be a vice-president on their suc- cessful year, and said he was proud to belong to a club which helped the inhabitants of the district to " play the game" as Englishmen and sportsmen. He then proceeded with the distribution of prizes. Songs were given at intervals by several of those present and a most enjoyable evening was passed

div.head: ODDFELLOWS ANNIVERSARY AT EARLFATOIVN.
div.p: ODDFELLOWS ANNIVERSARY AT EARLFATOIVN.

On Saturday evening the annual dinner and meeting in connectien with the Loyal Viaduct Lodge of Odrlfellows, was held at the Wellington Hotel, Earlw=town. There was a good muster, of members at the dinner, which was well served, and thoroughly enjoyed. At the subsequent meeting, PPGM Thomas Tunste,ll presided, and be was supported by Prov. (.3 it, T S Steel (Warrington) Prov. DG M Clare, (Warrington), PPGM John Tunstall (Liverpool), and PPG M Eckersley (Gol- borne). Ihe report of the secretary Bro Thane, given in response to the toast " The Viaduct Lodge," stated that the Actuary's valuation showed that there were two lodges with a consider- able surplus, viz, Ashton and Golborne. Newton Lodge had wiped out a large portion of its defici- ency, and the only one which had not, progressed as they would like, was Ilaydock. The district was in a very prosperous condition a: the prosent time. During the past 12 months he had to deplore an excess of sick pay. .£490 had been paid for sick and £7O for funeral fees, a total of £560. A number of speeches were delivered during the evening by Bros. Steel, Tunstall, and Clare, and songs were given at intervals by willow; members. YBoxeivnY CHURCH PARADE AT Nrirron. On Sunday, afternoon a military parade took place at St !Peter's Church, Newton-le-Willows, chiefly as a memorial service to the late Lord Gerard, Colonel of the Lancashire Hussars. There was a large number of the C Troop (Newton-le- Willows) of the Lancashire Hussars On parade,under the command of Lieutenant C T Street, and includ- ing several of the South African Warriors; a de- tachment of the 6th V B King's Liverpool Regiment, and another representing the let Seuth Lancashire V B Prince of Wales' hegiment. The Lancashire Hussars band was also present. A great throng of people crowded the streets. The organist (Ur Edwin Leyland) played the " Lost Chord "and Chopin's " Funeral March in splendid style in memory ot the late Colonel. The vicar (the Bev James Ryder),in the MUM othis remarks, made ' touching reference to the kindliness, bravery, and generosity of the late Lord Gerard. The service was a most impressive one, and the hymns Bung were those selected by Lady Gerard, viz, "Onward, Christian Soldiers,"" A day's march nearer home," and "Nearer, my God, to Thee The band en route and on the return played the marches which . were Lord Gerard's favourite compositions.

TO THE ELECI'ORS OF' FAIRFIELD WARD.

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, During my term of office as Town Councillor I have striven loyally to discharge the trust you so genemsly gave me three years ago. I am the candidate of the Conservative party and have been promised support by a numher of Liberal friends, In asking for your votes at the corning election I hope I may without offence, appeal to my record, and respect- fully invite the active support of all who value effici- ency, economy, and a laign standard of public life. Yours faithfully. ALleilkiD J. JOLLEY.
October 16th, 1902,

LA2CIIFORD WARD.
LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— Having been requested to stand as a Can- didate for your Ward, I beg to appeal to you for your support in returning me to serve your interests in the Town Council.
I have been a resident in the Labcaford Ward for the last sixteen years, and I have always publicly taken an interest In matters affecting the advancement of the Town.

If elected, my aim will be to exercise due care In Finance while maintaining efficiency, and to serve your interests with probity and zeal. Politically it is well known that I am a Con- servative,but in this contest I am an Independent Candidate and confidently venture to appeal to all ratepayers for their support and votes. I am ladies and gentlemen, Yours obediently, W. B. ROBERTS. Wilderspcol, Oct 15, 1932.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. ______ • WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCIETY.
div.p: THE OUR LOCAL CHURCHES. ______ • WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCIETY.

There was'an average attendance at the meeting of this society on Sunday afternoon. The chair was occu- pied by Mr Benjamin Farrar (hoe secretary). In refer- ring to the membership of the society, he expressed the leepe that the total of 59.8 which was reached last half year would be exceeded in the present half year. Men- tion was also made of the successful inauguration of the Holidays' Savings Club, which already had a member- ship of 89. Mr Alfred Corney delivered an address. He observed that as the harvest festival of that church was lbeing held that day, he thought it would be fitting if he spoke upon a subject connected with the harvest. He was not speaking about the material harvest which had already been gathered in but a harvest that was growing in the heart of humanity He referred to the harvest the Psalmist of old spoke of when he said "Truth shall spring up out of the earth and righteousness look dovris from Heaven." In elaborating his theme, Mr. Comes? said there seemed to he in each one of us two lives—the eerthly life with its daily avocations and common work ; and the higher life to which belonged our highest asniratioes and deepest 1 hopes, and our great ideals. These twe parts of our manhood made up one life of harmony. It was imoos- sih!e to separate the world of thought from the world of action ; the two belonged to eaeh other. Ideals, be showed, served a great purpose, when they were put into action. The men who had moved their fellow-men Blest were theca who had beeo possessed of great ideets ; men who saw the eternal righteousness looking dawn fro eaven. Practical lit o must perish and become pata'yzed in the state, in the church and in the indivi- dual unless men i kept the 'ideal life before them to inspiee and uplift them. There had been on this earth a life perfect and complete—% life noon which eternal righteousness looked down and was well pleesed—and that was the life of Christ. Mr Coney proceeded to show that we never could live this higher life unless we moaned oar hearts to Cheiet. A. r.r.icatinn ontVind "The Road to Heaven" was effectively given by Miss 0w.,,

BUCKLEY-STREET METHODIST FREE CHURCH. Mr Pinches of Chester, preached the anniversary eer- mons in the above place of worship on Sunday. In the morning he took his text from Acts ii. 2, " And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty ceind,and it filled all the hens° where they were sitting." Is the evening, Mr Pipcnes discoursed upon the words " Blessed are they that do his commandments,that they may leave right to the Tree of Life, and may enter in throuele the gates into the city " (Rev ed. 14). The I services were well attended throughout the day. Special hymns were sung and the entheme " Give unto the Lord, oye Kinedom "and " In the shadow of the Almighty," wore carefully rendered by the chair, under the leadership of Mr J Ryder. A musical service was held in the afternoon, presided ever by Mr Pirushee,Misa Wilson gave ft clear expression of" 0 rest in the Lord," and Mr J Harman's tenor voice was heard to advantage in 'he solo "If with all your hearts." " A Dream " was the title of the clarionst solo given by Mr A Taylor. Mr A Bares creditably rendered two violin solos. Mr Albert E Trim was the accompanist. The Rev H Dunnico gave an address on "Is life worth living ?" in the ceuree of which he said that while evolutionists were always trying to make out where they came from, and while theologians were al mays trying to make out where they were going to, they were both agreed on the fact of their existence in this world. A great mystery surrounded their creation and their exit from this world, many believing that as they lived in this world, either to God or Co the devil .so in the time to come they would either receive the blessings or the curses of eternity. "Is thie life worth living " asked the rev. gentlemes, and in order to get an answer he would ask them ts study the opinien of Solomon and Jeremiah, and other leading Filen in the Bible, and they would find that even in the Bible there was a difference of eniniea - Co whether life was re tlly worth living. If they dould make life worth living he thought they would do I well to follow the advice he would offer th-m—they should cirry the divineet motives ieto the ceincneeisst acts and the lowliest duties of every-day life. They should learn to see God eyeryis here, and they should make a whole-hearted consecration of their lives to the service of Christ.
I pn iAeroul

div.head: EMMANUEL CHURCH. WARRINGTON. SERMONS BY THE NEW MINISTER.
div.p: EMMANUEL CHURCH. WARRINGTON. SERMONS BY THE NEW MINISTER.

There were good eongregetions at Emmanuel Chureh Warrington, on Sunday when the Rev Arthur G D Gee the newly-appointed minister preached his opening sermons. Mr Gee has left the Established Church " through the prevalence," to use his own words, " of Sacordotalism and the neglect of the Evangelical party as a whole to make any effective protest thereto." In his sermons he did not make any sllusions to Cols, defor- ring any statement of his position as to the Established Church till after his installation, shortly to take place, by the Right Rev Bishop Eldridge. In the morning he took ae his text the words "0, L -ad revive now Thy work in the midst of the years." fle painted out hew God 'ned answered th,, prayer of the Prophet, particularly in the great revival of spiritull religion in the days of the Restoration of the remnant of the Jews. He showed how tbe great characteristics of this religious a wakening were, firstly, the honouring of the Word of aod ; secondly, tha confession of sin ; and, thirdly, the putting away of evil ; and stated that these features characterized evene true spiritual revival. After refer- ring to the need of a frelb outpouring of the Holy Spirit on the Church at the present time,he spoke of the causes of spiritual declension in the individual, and the ways of reviving the spiritual life. The preacher closed by showing the imperfection of all reyiyala in this dispense- tinn. stating that only when the Saviour cams again would his work be for ever reviyed.—ln the evening the Rev A G D Gee preached from the teat " Him that cemoth unto me I will in no wise east out." The service was hearty and encouraging for the suceoss of the new ministry.

Dr T. FT. Smith. Wiyal Cl.,iiil Zrstituto.North umber land Avenue, W.C., writes :—" I have much pleasure in teetifying te the superior qustities of Vi-Cocoa over any similar preparation in the market. I do this willingly acdunsolicited.as I:cousider it a:great Luisa to the public. Its wonderful recuperative power after exhaustion from fatigue i 3 marvellous."

div.head: gHARVEST
div.p: gHARVEST
wYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CPIURCH.

Harvest thanksgiving services were held is Wycliffe Congregational Church on Sunday• The pastor (Rev JO'm Yong) preached morning and eveniog to large congregations,that in the evening being especially large. No attempt was made to decorate the church, the ladies confining themselves to the display of a choice selection of flowers and ferns on the communion table. The preacher based his discourse at the naorning service on the text "I will sing unto the Lord as long as I Hoe ; I will sing praise to my G3l while I have my being ". Ira alluding to the common notion that harvest thanksgiving was confined to a special service, the preacher pointed Gut that harvest festivals were not thanksgivings unless they had their Roarce ani warrant in au habitual arose of gratitude and in- ward praisefulness of spirit. Toe preacher pro- ceeded to 3ho w that the religious temperament if gratitude and praise, if only sought for, could be lb- tained as the result of intelligent thought and prayer and effort. Let the thankfulnesa for the harvest, he said, stimulate the perpetual thankfulness and praise- fulnem of their whole lives. Let their lives be attune to praise Him who bleved them every day.—The obeir, under the conductorship of Mr W El Payton, :des. BAC., sang the anthem "0 taste and see" (Gass). Mr Z iba Armitage, the hen treasurer. in referring to the collec- tions which wore being taken that day on behalf of the ! ecritingent fund, announced that £34 were still required ' I. enable the church to start the new finasicial year with a clean balance sheet.—At night, the e‘meregatien was greatly Inconvenienced by a temporary failure of the gas suoply. Only a faint glimmer ceuld be oh- tairod at some of the gas brackets, whilst at others there was no supply of gas at all. Two large ail lemons were introduesd into the pulpit and lighted up that end of the church. When the service corn- mowed the church W 35 in semi-darkness, and some time ' elapsed before a meter inspector from the Gas Vl,Grke suaceeded in remedying the siefeet. A short stoppage was then made for the purpose of lighting up, and to remainder of the service was completed in comfort. The preacher based his discourse en the words " While the earth remaioeth harvest snail not cease." Genesis:Ba., 22 verse. They were met that night, he said, . to thank Ged for an abundant harvest, by which the physical necessities of every one of them ware met by the bounty of His graciens good- ness. The harvest of 1902 was one more illustration of the Divine Creator's faithfulness to promise, faith-
EXAMINER FRIDAY OCTOBER 24 1902

fulners to the knowledge of the needs of his creatures, faithfulness to human well-being. Let them Ise reminded, of how this ingathered harvest spoke to them supremely about God. Let it speak to them of the fact that there was a time of sowing and a t ms of reapmg. They were reminded than their own iudivid aal lives would have a harvest, and their personal harvest whether material, moral or spiritual,would be the issue of their own sow- ing. The festival character of that thanksgiving should make them desirous that their personal harvest in this life should be a season of rejoicing,jcongratulation and thankfulness.—Two anthems were contrahot id by toe choir narnely,"Be glad and rejoin" (Myles B Forster) and " The eyes of all wait anon Ittee,o Lord"(G T Evey), the solo in the first named being taken by Mr J T Knowles. Harvest hymns were sung, and the service throughout the day were cf a very successful character

div.head: CHAIRMAN AND THE 13- )YCOTT
div.p: THE CHAIRMAN AND THE 13- )YCOTT

The CiesialteN, in moving the adoption of the report, said the sales had receded somewhat from those of the previous quarter, but that was explained by the fact that the past quarter w as always the lean quarter of the year. It was the vertsr in which most people tied their holidays. Everybody was spending a goad deal of money sam-where else and si he supposed it reacted in this way. If they compared the sales of the past quarter with those of a year agc they would See that they *mounted to £2,100 more. It would be rernem-, bared that at the last quarterly meeting they sanctioned a gift of £5OO to the Infirmary and Dispensary. That gift, he (Mr Birchen) had the pleasure of presenting to the Infirmary Committee a few weeks ago and he ceuld assure the members that it wan received with gratitude and enthusiasm. The Secretary had written a letter stating that at a meeting of the Board of Management it was decided that the beet thanks of the Board be given to the Warrington Industrial Co-operative Society, for their magnificent gift of £5OO made in commemoration of the C monition of King Elward VII., and that a memorial tablet be placed in one of the weeds as a parmenent memorial of the generosity of the S (Applause).. Continuing, the Chairman said a statement was made at a meeting of the Warrington District Nursing Asso- ciatioa that a sum of £250 might be obtained from the Co-operative Society towards the purchase of a horns. As co-operators they believed the Nursing Association to he an excellent iuctitatien, but they were not pre- pared at present to make the contribution suggested. No doubt many of them would have seen that there was a great ferment aad stir eceag on iu the country with regard to co-operation. Trade,* were takine alarm and had made up their minds, very foolishle he thought, to fight the co-operative societies. They (the co-operators) were not in the least afraid. They were quite prepared to take the private traders on any ground Ithey liked. The Ce-eperetive Union was determined to raise a fund of £lOO,OOO to combet the ooycott. The Wholesale Rerietv had guaranteed £50,000 and the various societies were each doing their share towards guaranteeing the remainder. If any co-operative mem- ber was punished by losing his employment for being al member of the co-eperativa society, they would have a 1 fund to fall tack upon and legal advice was being taken as to whether they could bring the offenders into the law courts and punish them for this iniquitous and unreasonable conduct. The boycott amounted to the suggestion that working men had no right to speed their money where they liked. He be- lieved working ma would not stead that sort of thing and would retort smartly on those who practised it. (Hear, hear.) The committee suggested that that meet- ing should be asked to guarantee £lOO towards the central fund. In making that sugeestien the committee had certainly net overstepped the mark. They were determined to defend their rights in this matter. (Hear, hear.) Their position was a strong one and be believed it would make them take a greater interest ha muni- cinal electione. It had had that effete; at St [doles.. There the sweaty had nominated two candidates in the persons of the vice-president and the manager (Mr Winterbottorn) to fight two of the traders for seats on the Town Connell They (the co-operators) had en many reseurcee behind them that they could snap their fingers at these people and tell them to do their worst. Mr. E. ENGLAND thought the Warrington Society might guarantee a !weer sum than £lOO. The society was much stronger than appeered on the balance sheet, sate he would eueeeet that a guarantee of £350 be made. (Hear, hear.) He halievei that the trading objection to me-eparativistn was wrong in prinaiple and most foolish in practice. He believed it would result in great good to the co-operative movement. He believed ce-opora- tints was one of the solutions of the difficulties between capital and lahenr and be would like to see the principles of co-operation brought more effectively: into business generally. :Efearesear.) Mr JEFFREY said the cemmittee had had the question of a gum ranting to the central ,funel under seriaus con- sideration. While £lOO seemed a vary small sum to eller antee,it must net be forgotten that there were over 1.200 eocietiee in Enelamd and if each guaranteed £lOO there would be raised £120,000 which together with the Whelesale Society's contribution of £50,000 would make £170,000. That was a great deal more than would be required. He did not see the advantage of making a great prornese for the sake of the aupearanen Of tbn thine. If necessity required it, the Warriagton Society eould easily contribute £5OO. It was for the members to say what guarantee should ha made, bee the COP:I2- mitteP theught £lOO was sufficient for the preeent. The Omar/men said it .47£1.S pessible that some societies could not guarantee anything. It was necessary to Make a bold front in these matters. Mr CSOWTFIBR matted out that the Runcarri Society had guaranteed £3OO and he thought a guarantee of at least £250 was little eneueh for a society like Warring- ton. _ .

Mr B FARRAR thollelt thi gittjinagainSt the Co- operative movement would die rs natural death and that Ithe money would mot be reclaim/. Be WA3 in favour of the eeirimittee's recommendation. Mr William LOWE remarked that the central organiza- tion had suggested a contribution of one shilling per member and he did not think they were doing their duty if they did less than that. Be wao in favour of a grant of £250. After further di.cuasion it was decided to guarantee £lOO for the present and the committee was empowered to increase it to £5OO if nocessary. In answer tit a question, the SECRETARY said the member4bip of the Society was new 6,001. The report was unanimously adopted. div.head: NEW BAPTISI MINISI ER ORDAINED.
div.p: NEW BAPTISI MINISI ER ORDAINED.
Services at Golborne Street.
Rev. Dr. Aked and Noncomformist Liberty

Golborne-street Baptist Church was the scene of two interesting gatherings oniThursday last week on the occasion of the ordination and recognition of the pas tor (Rev Herbert Dunnico). In the afternoon, the charge to the minister was given by the Rev Professor Bumby, 8.A., of Nottingham University College, and the Rev Dr Aked, of Liverpool, de- livered the charge to the church. The chair *-as isecupiA by Mr Hoff ham, of Bir- mingham and he was accompanied on the rostrum by the ministers from neighbouring towns, includ- ing the previous pastor the Rev J T Schofield. After a hymn had been sung and prayer offered, a statement Wa4' read by the Secretary of the Church (Mr. Buckby) relating the circumstances which led to Mr Dunnico accepting the call to the pastorate of the church.

The Rev Profemor Bunny, in deliverine the e.harge to the minister,pointed on'. that they who were called upon at times to give cherges to their younger brethros, did net speak as t lough they had attained any perfectness themselves, but they would fair. give their younger brethren the benefit of the lessons they had learnt from their experieeces to sive them from committing some of the mistakes that they who were older had per- chance made. The profeesor proceeded to base his charge te the minister on the ;paseages contained in the first three voiles of the net chapter of Isaiah. He advised the minister to let it be his first prayer and first care that the spirit of the Lord was his. Let him make his calling sure first as a man Man could not give the cell': God must give it. There were some people who thought that it was easier for a Christian minister te lead a Christian life. He would not say that familiarity with holy things breeds contempt, but he did say that familiarity with the most sacred things tended, lest they were jealous to keep all things in sub- ordination, to callous indifference. He knew few perils greater than that of a wrong view of an orlittation ser- vice. The professor proceeded to explain that ordina- tion was an act of God -, it was not something which man could do for the minister. Let the minister remember thLt his strenet's was wholly from God and let him see to it that his heart was a fit dwelling-place for the Spirit of God. In alluding to the necessity of a minister ever being a student, Professor Buneby po,nted out that Gil had used unc altered men to achieve mighty results. He had used them in spite of their ignorance, not because of it. Other things being equal these aims werild have done greater things if their minds had been trained. The minister of to-day nowt ever seek to keep his mind trained and exercised. He must study earnestly, study closely, study because it fitted his mind to grapple with the great preblemenhat must come before him. There would inevitably be around him in the homes of his people cultured and active young men who would very soon I iarn to know whether he had a mind cultured and cultivated, and if he had not, if :he showed less mental power and less mental grasp than thee were acsuetomed to see in their business houses, or found him lax or negligent, could they reasonably expect them to believe in his exposition of God's word ? Let the minister keep the light burn- ing in his study, but do not let him confuse the study with the nulpit. It was his business to grapple with the great questions that exercised the minds and hearts of 1 the most thoughtful of men, and to digest what he had read before he ventured to give it to his people. There were some things it might be better to keep in the study than in the polpit. The Profess n• proceeded to advise the preacher to preach Christ, and to think of his privi- leges and responsibilities. The Rev FISRBERT DIINNICO thanked Professor Thereby fin his kind words and said the exigencies of time made it necessary for him tolreserve his response to the change! until the evening meeting. Referring th the presence of the Rev Dr Aked, Mr Donnie° observed that if he was only able to do for Warrington a tithe of what Dr Aker] I had done for Liverpool be should feel he had not lived his life in vain,

Sdadame 1411313)NE gave au excellent interpretation of the solo " Lead kindly light." The Rev Dr AKED then deliveral the charge to the churoh. and at the outset referred to the solemn and memorable character of the meeting. If that meeting was momentous and memorable for them, it was also well to remember that it was being held in a moment of our English history, momentous and mernerable too. The present was an hour of crisis and judgment for the whole of the Protestant religion of this country and of the English liberties which we revered. They were Free Churchmen and met together as a free church.Tnere was no earthly crown and no human statesman who could appoint their brother to be the minister of that church. The Free Churches stood for free men and they stood for free nations and in this hour theywere called upon by all the forces outside them and by the deepest implications of their being to stand once more for liberty. They I were face to face with the most sinister attack upon 1 their Nonconformity that had been made since the act of uniformity was passed. They were called upon once again to stand for the protestentism of the Protestant religion and assert once more the crown rights of Bing Jesus as against the intervention of the priests. They mast not forget they were met together as Baptists. He found the Baptist to be the man of all men who stood solidest in his shoes. On many a field of battle and blond the banner of civil end religions liberty had been borne aloft by Baptist hands. Let them never dream that he would ask them to put themselves in a condition of enthusiasm if the issue was merely a silly squabble about little water and no water or whether it were, wise to din or sprinkle. Whenever they found a Baptist who knew why he was a Baptist there they found a stickler for human liberty ; there they found a man who was a centre and force of social, political ani civic activity, devoted to the uplifting of the common manhood of common ' men. (Hear, heir). They were called upon in this hour to stand for the nrotestantism of the protestant faith and'for the freedom of the Free Church,of free term and free nations. (Applause). Gathered on one ef the solemnest occa,ions which could call a church together, let this be one of the impulses et their life that they would come out to do bottle for human liberty, to safe- guard the heritage which they had received from the men whe won it for them. (Applause.) If they were ton spiritual for the work of social and political redemption their spirituality was of the wrong sett. (Hear, hear.) What were churches for ? As a church they Must tand for hum in freedom, as a Church they must stand for the right of individual souls to come direct to the crucified and risen Christ,and as'a church they must stand for the liberty of the church from every form of outside domination and control. The 1 church had to kill the public-house and unless they were on that side their spirituality was not worth having. A Liverpool authority heti told them more than once before the public, that in his solemn judgment the public-houee damned tea souls for every one that all the churches saved. The duty of the church was to destroy the liquor traffic with the native races abroad and te kill the public-houses•at home. Dr Aked proceeded to refer to the gambling evil and said it was the duty of the Christflan church te sweep the evil away. Us would not discuss methods of dealing with the crying horror of human poverty. There were those 1 amongst them who believed that competition was the last 1 word God bad to speak to a nation,but who believed that competition needed to be purified. There were also those who did not think competition was God's last word, but 1 wholoelieved that co-operation, brotherhood and loye 1 1 would be better than competition. He would not discuss the methods of dealing with the poverty and misery of life but he insisted that it was the duty of the Church te find out the cause of poverty and to sweep away that which degraded, debased and demoralised man, and to uplift human life. Unless the church real- ised that as part of its essential duty then the church had not realised the call of God He pleaded with them forpoyalty to theie minitter in every effort that he made lin the direction of human redemption ; loyalty to him in every single stroke of work that tended to the cleansiee of men's minds, the cleansing of ; men's home!, and the improvement of the cenditions un de- 'which men lived. It was not the enemy in front that troubled the minister, it was the shaky friends behind him. (Hear, hear). The world would never be saved except by Jesus Christ. It was 1 for Him that they were going to win the kingdoms of this world. They were going to win the press for Christ ; they were going to win the Town Council for Chris's ; they were going to drive the publican off the Town C emeil in the name of Jeeus Chris and they were going to prevent

the representatives of the IL, toe Dame Warrington ruling the affairs of the tow, dgteauc, eLI art of Christ they claimed all literature, sham. Curiae tot and all the activities of man and nett for tue world, the town, Christ for the nation, Christfied tee motive Christ the head of all, and Christ cruel y duGioa. of every thought and the spring of ever plause.)
