div.head: TEIE EVENING MEETING.
div.p: TEIE EVENING MEETING.

There WAS a crowded congregation at the public meeting in the evening. The chair was taken by Mr Bamforth, and amongst those present were :--Rev Pro- fessor Bumby' 8.A., Rev H Minnie°, Rev J T Schofield, of Leeds, ReyT 8 Hughes, Rev J E Roberts. M.A., 8.D., Rev H V Thomas, Rev Thomas Hamer and others. Letters of apology for non-attendance were read by Mr Buckley (church secretary) from several rev, gent men, including Professor Bowser, M.A. Dr. Macular le- and the Rev John Yonge. en. T:ie CHAIRMAN, in the course of an interesting address said it was a little over twelve menthe ago since they bade farewell to their late pester, Mr Schofield, whom they were pleased to see with them that night. (Hear, hear.) Mr Sehofield laid the foundation which had made the Success of Galborne-3treet church possible. For many years Golborne-street had been under a aloud and he had sometimes sorrowfully consoled himself with the thought that all other Noncon- formist chutehes were likewise under a cloud. (Laughter). They all recognised that Mr Dun- niche in accepting the pastorate was making a sacri- fice, for other churches in a better pesition were open for his acceptacce. It had already been said that if Mr Dunnico made a success of Golberne-street he would perform a miracle. (Laughter.) Re (the Chairman) hoped Mr Dunnice would receive nothing but sympa- thetic encouragement, not only from the members of that church but from all gee other churches in the town. (Rear, hear.) Since alr'Dunnico came amongst them ' they had done splendidly. At the nutset they raised £3O as a second contrihutinn to the 20:h Century Fund, making a total for thee church of almost £BO. They had also raised £lOO hr the renovation and restoration of the church, and only £2O was required to pay off the debt. They had increased the weekly offerings ad raised £2O by a harvest festival. They had practically doubled tho congrega. tiers, and mere than once they had been crowded out. They had also commenced a Weenesday evening service and obtained an average attendance of 90 people. A Bible class had also been started with an average attendance of 60. There were added, or there were waiting to be added 11 or 12 names to the church roll. That, he thought, was not a bad record for the few months sine, Mr Donnie') settled amongst them. They required £5OO towards new siehools—(hear, hear,) —and they were hoping to get it some time next year. He did act mention that as a criterion of what they were going to do or as a boast of what they had done. He trusted that Mr Duenico's ministry would not only be a blessing el that church but to every institution in the towo. (Hear, hear). Professor EIIMBY in the course of an address, said he I believed he made almost his first attempt at preaching in Warrington. It was made in a very hunob'e way in connection with Wycliffe mission. That was nearly twenty years ago and it was very nice to revisit the scenes of one's early experiences. He wished to plead earnestly with them to encourage Mr Dunnico in his work and to "exercise the imagination in the interest of charity." It was not the minister's task to fill the chnrch,but it was the minister's duty to give the prop's something to carry away- The Rev THOMAS HAMER spoke of his knowledge of Mr Dunnico when a boy and young man in coauection with hie church at Nottingham. Rev B ROBERTS, moderator of the Lancashire and Cheshire Association and the Rev H V Thomas (secre- tary), also addressed words of encouragement to the church and their new minister. The Rey U Droeteteolin alluding to a remark made by Mr!Thomas,said Golborne-street did not want any help from the Association to carry on the ordinary church work, but the need of new buildings was imperative and when the time came, the Laacashire and Cheshire Associetion would probably help them. (Hear, hear.) The Rev J T SCHOFIELD said be came from Leeds to Warrington not with the intention of making a speech but rather with the intention of renewing his acquaint- enc. with many friends in connection with the church. That church had often been in hie mind and its welfare had been the subject of his prayers. Ile had regarded it rather as a compliment to himself that they were doing so well at Golborne-street. (Rear, hear). He had been very glad indeed to hear of the signs of blessing that had rested upon the short ministry of Mr Dunnico. He hoped Mr Duanice'e labours would be abundantly successful and that there would grow up a strong Baptist church there to the glory of God. (Applause). • Another solo was efficiently sung by Madame Rath- bens.

The Rev HERBERT HUNNICO, who had a very cordial reception, alluded to the helpful address which wss addressed to him by Professor flumby,and to the words of sound advice and good counsel which it contained. Four years ago when he had his farewell gathering prior to going to college, he was told that he was a man of great courage for giving up good busi- ness prospect. in sneer to enter the Christian ministry at a time when preaching wag at a discodnt. He (Mr Dunnloo) did net believe preaching was at a discount. (Hear. bear.) He believed the heart of humanity was craving for the gospel and he believed soy man who brought the living message from a living Ged would never lack people veld were willing to listen to him. (Hear, pear.) He was there to become their minister bemuse he found theta was no higher work in this world than to tell to weary men and women the store of Christ and lead weary lonia into • a haven of peace. Proceeding to speak of his past career, Mr Dunnico referred to the first twelve years of hie life as being spent in fellowship with the Church of England, five years of which time be Was a chorister. He afterwards became very much attached to the Congregational Church and found scope for work under the pastorate of the Rev Thomas Hamer to whom he owed much. Alluding to his acceptance of the pastorate at Golborns- street. Mr Dunnioo said be could net wish for a bet,er set of officers or a more self-sacrificing people than he had there. Re would like to thank them for the confidence they had placed in him. They placed no restrictions on him : they did not want to know whether he was orthodox or heterodox. He came on the condition that ic the pulpit they gave him perfect liberty. He did not think they had always agreed with him, but he thought they bad recognised his sincerity and believed that be was endeavouring to givie the troth. He did not think they would have obtained the large congregations they had succeeded in gathering,if they bad attempted to gag him. If they did attempt to gag him he would leave them for ever. He believed in the deity and divinity of Christ and be believed Christ was the only hope for a .fallen world. Apart from that he hound himself to nothing. He would ask the church to be loyal and true to him. If ever he left Warrington it would be their own fault. As long es they found him some work In do he was there to do , it. (Applause.) Mr B FEW propoaed a vote of thank g to those wh had a.siated in any way et the gathering.
, Mr ROFFHAM, of Birmingham, mended the proposi- tion. which was unaniertougly agreed to. Tho meeting, which hal been a dscply interesting one, then terminated.

Mr C S Burgess presided over a larg„f attendance. The lecturer gave a brief history the English Church front the year 697 to 902. 1110 contended that there • could be no possible that there bad been one continuous body. div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.

Coming Events. Our readqrs will notice by an announcement in our advertising columns, that on Monday evening next, a meeting will be bold in Parr Hall. Warring- ton, under the auspices of the Diocesan Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society, when addressee will be delivered by the Archdeacon of Warrington (The Van T J Madden), the Rev Richard Postance, Vicar of St George's, Everton (and Chairman of the Diocesan Branch) and Alder- man W J Burgess, J.P , of Liverpool who was formerly a town councillor at Warrington. The Rector of Warrington, the Rev Canon Willis will preside.

South Lancashire Tramways. The trams on the Leigh route of the South Lanca- shire Tramways Company's system commenced running on Monday for public traffic. At five o'clock in the morning special cars ran for the accommodation of workmen going to their work, and these cars were well patronised. A regular and frequent service of cars will be kept up between Lowton, Leigh, Howe Bridge, and Atherton to Bol- ton. During the day the cars carried a good num- ber of passengers; and, as they are comfortable, well lighted, and commodious, will prove a great boon to the inhabitants of the district. A Stockton Heath Publican's Sudden Death. At a quarter to seven on Saturday evening Mr Richard Newell, landlord of the Mulberry Tree Inn, Stozkten Heath, was serving in the bar, when he wit- seized with an attack of apoplexy. Dr Parker was summoned, and seeing that Mr Newell's con- dition was serious, he sent for the assistance of Dr Joseph. Mr Newell, however, expired in a few minutes, before Dr Joseph's arrival. Deceased, who was about 55 years of age, is survived by his wife, two sons and two daughters. He formerly carried on business as a pawnbroker off Oxford- street, Manchester,but had lived at Stockton Heath for the last two years. He purchased the Mulberry Tree Inn, which he conducted as a free house, An inquest was not deemed necessary. The Young Helpers' League. On Saturday afternoon a meeting of the members of the "Young Helpers' League" in connection with the National Waifs' Association (Dr Barnado's Homes) was held in Toft's Assembly Room, Friars' Green. Miss Rice. the warden for this district,was present to formally open the " Habitation." She gave a very interesting address to the young people explaining to them the great work Dr Barnado does in looking after the orphan crippled and in- capable poor children, The Habitation has been formed during the last twelve months and 30 mem- bers are now on the roll. A. branch lodge has also been opened at Stockton Heath. It is hoped that in time as the League grows, Warrington will be able to support a" cot "of its own, which will be called the " Warrington cot."

div.head: SEQUEL TO AN ACCIDENT AT MESSRS. RYLANDS BROS.
div.p: SEQUEL TO AN ACCIDENT AT MESSRS. RYLANDS BROS.

Before His Honour Judge B3wen Rowlands at the I Warriagton County Court on Thursday, Messrs Rylands Bros applied to review and terminate or diminish an agreement made between them and Frederick William Price, Oid Chapel Cottages Padgate, under the Work. men's Compensation Act for the payment at 103 5d per week.—Mr Brooks of Messrs Chapman and Brooks, solicitors,Manchester represented the applicants and Mr Cuthbert Smith (instructed by Mr TS Steel, Warrington) I appeared for the respondent. The facts of the case are that on the 12th February, 1902, Price was in the employ of the applicants at their works in Church-street as a wire weaver, working on a 4 inch netting 10-,no. Nitnlst engaged in his work his right band caught in the machine, and his hand and fore-arm were so severely crushed that both had to be amputated. The Company on the 30th May entered upon an agrAment, under the Workmen's Compensa- tion Act, to pay Price half his average earaings, 10i sd! per week. The firm had continued to pay that sum, ! and had since offered Price the position of lodge-keeper and time.keeper at their new works at Dalton Bank, but Price declined the offer, feeling nit be would not be able to perform the du lea, and the sitaation had since been filled. Mr Brooks rated that the firm of Rylands Bros. took a great interest in Price acd bad ealielidepl a great deal of sympathy towards him. Ire April they were enabled to offer him the po.sition of folitman, the duties con- nected with which were very Ilgtii—only requiring a little writing—and such as could be easily undertaken by Price, For this work they were prepared to pay Price 251 per week; a higher rate of wages than ho earned before the accident. Price w mid not accept that situation though it was offered to him many times and left open for him for several months. Mr Brooks pull in all the correspondence connected with the case and contended that by reason of the offer they had made to Price plaintiffs were entitled to a re- duction in the amount of the weekly payment. Mr John James Niell, works manager for the appli- cants, said that the duties of lodw-keaaier were suah as could be ably discharged by the respondent. Respondent bad never attempted to discharge those duties though he had on several occasions said he would do so. Mr Brooks contended that the ma a was not anxious to resume work. Mr Niell was cross-examined at length by Mr Smith Be denied calling upon the respondent and offering him £5O in settlemen'" of the case. That amount WAS offered by the Insurance Company. He could not give evidence as to anything which might have occured be- tween Mr Hulse (secretary of the company) and Mr Steel. Price was quite prepared to rstura to work until be was seen by Mr. Steel. Before witnesses were called by Mr Smith, his Honour remarked that he did not vita see how the applicants bad made out this case.. . . . .

Dr. Ferguson was called and said he had examined Price that day. In his opinion respondent was not flt to do the work required of him as quickly as was nece!- nary. Frederick William Price,the respondent,gave evidence and denied that he was unwilling to do the work or that Mr Steel prevented him. The post at the lodge was offered to him a considerable time after he had consulted Mr Steel. Owing to the injury las was at present unable to wash himself or to fasten his tie. Cross-examined by Mr Brooks: He told the firm that he could not possibly do the work. Mr Steel gave evidence with regard to the correspond- ence which bad passed in connection with the case. It was ebgolutely untrue that he prevented Price from takpag, a situation. Price told him all along that he thought he could not perform the duties. Mr Smith contended that it would be impossible for • one-armed man to discharge the duties of lodge -keeper. Mr BROOKS submitted that the reason why Price would not accent the situation was that be wanted the lump sum of £l5O. In giving judgment his Honour said he thought. Messrs fivlands Bros had evinced a very fair interest in Price and a desire to meet the neceesities A the case From the evidence submitted be was of the opinion that it would have been utterly fade for the respondent to have attempted -the work. The very mention of the duties he would have to perform was enough for him (his Honour) to agree with the conten- tion that they were of such a character that they would not have been satisfactorily performed by the respond- ent. Applicants hid not satisfied him that Price was able to earn any appreciable sum and be refused the application with costs on scale B.
ALTON S ACTIVE. SERVIE VI :N.

Public Welcome Home and Presentation. The Ha:nu 'detachment of active service men were entertained to a note° pie sup .)er in the Girl'd School, Halton, on Saturday evening and were subsequently presented with watches suitably inscribed. The coat was defrayed from a public fund. There was a repre- sentative attendance at the supper, which was well- catered for by Mr Walker, of the Castle Hotel. A concert was afterwards held. The Vicar (the Rev G D. Wray) presided, and there Were also present—Dr Carruthers and Ildessra A Furey, A Woodier, J S Jeacock,R Hughes, W Moores, J B Houghton, 8 Barrow. G H Hulme and J Looker. The names of the active service men are 1 Thomas Dunbebin, Thomas Newport, Henry Harrison, George London, and Fryer. During an interval in the entertainment,
I

The Vicar said in addition to entertaining the men and presenting watches to them out of the public fund, it was suggested that an honour list with their names should be put in the village hall. At a meeting on ' Thursday, however, the committee decided, if agreeable to those present, to restore the village cross and have , the names of the men inscribed upon it. (Hear, hear). fie had had put into his hand a most interesting photo- graph showing what the village was like in 1656 and in- cluding the village cross. Speaking for himself he , theueht the suggestion that they should restore the ' village cross was a most excellent one. (Hear, hear). It would commemorate better than an honour list in the village hall the part their friends had taken in the South African war. (Applause). They gave a very hearty welcome to their friends. He would like to repeat what be said before the men wect out and it was that when the men returned they should not be content with offer- ing them a welcome, but should, as a nation, do some- thing in the direction of paying their soldiers better. (Applause). Tte question rested largely with the work- ing people of the country, and if they demanded that our soldiers should be paid a proper wage it would come to pass. (Applause). The Vicar then read an interest- ing statement setting forth the career of several local soldiers, and in calling upon Dr Carruthers to present the watches expressed regret that Mrs Carruthers was unable through illness to be present. Dr Carruthers,who was very heartily received, said he was sorry Mrs Carruthers was unable to be present, as he knew it wouid have given her much pleasure to present the watches. The honour of doing se,therefore, devolved upon him. Thr y were all proud of their Army and Navy, and teey were especially proud of their fellow villagers who had served their King and country in the late war. (Applause.) It was with the greatest pleasure that they welcomed them back again safe and sound, and hoed they would accept these watches: as a slight token or the esteem in which they beide:such gallant defenders of our country. (Applause.) He wished them all good luck and health and prosperity in times both of peace and war, and trusted that the watches would have as much go and staying power in thernae they and their fellow soldiers had shown. (Applause.) Messrs London, Dunbebin an" Newport, upon :receiv- ing their watches, made a suitable acknowledgment of the villagers' appreciation of their services, and soldier- like averred that they had only done their duty. Fryer and Harrison are still away on services, and their ' watches were handed over to their relatives Mr Jeacock proposed a vote of thanks to Dr Cerrathers, for presenting the watches. Mr Hughes seconded and the vote was cordially carried. The Vicar read the following message from Mrs Carruthers :—" Please express to the soldiers of the Kele how much I regret being unable to present the watches, and offer them my heartiest congratulation upon their safe retina from the front. (Applause.) The committee's recommendation to restore the villager cross was then put to the meeting, and unani- mously carrel. An excellent entertainment was provided by Mrs Ellison, Miss Woode, Miss Watson, and Messrs ElliSnl). Walker, and Water's,. The accompanists were Arise Walker and Mrs W Ellams.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS,
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS,
Rugby Football.
[By Ovalistl

Warrington's performance on Saturday was distinctly creditable to the Club, for they admizustered the first check to ' the leaders of the Competition on their own ground. Every other opponent of the Halifax team has " gone under" very submissively, but not so Warrington. The " Wirepullers " are proving them- selves to be made of sterner stuff this season, and fully represented they will trouble any team in the Union. On Saturday they went away with a firm determination to defeat the " blue and whites "in their own citadel, and earn glory and some extra Rudos at one and the same time. They just failed in their aspirations, but, seeing that they shared the honours, we must be satis- fied with what was unquestionably a creditable performance.

Mr Neil, the president of the Warrington Club takes an increasingly keen interest in the doings of the team and on Saturday he went away with the players in order to encourage them in their effort to make proud Halifax bow the knee. He even intended, I believe,to make a special present to the man who crossed the hitherto—and still—unbroken Halifax goal-line first,but this was not communicated to the players beforehand,or selfish play rpight have ensued. Unfortunately, War- rington just failed to cross that formidable bit of white- wash and no one was more sorry than the President.

There was a fine crowd to welcome the team which has always given Halifax a good game,and the spacious ground at Hanson-lane was surrounded by a,solid ring of spectators numbering about 9,000. The best of foot ball weather favoured the fixture, and the ground being also in good order there were no drawbacks to a fast game. Both sides were well represented, Warrington having their picked team, and Halifax playing two sub- stitutes whose abilities were probably as great as those of the original selections And a fast game it proved, the teams being exceedingly well matched and strain- ing every nerve to secure the advantage. Warrington's keenness seemed to inspire the homesters, for they showed no laggardliness,and the play right through was more suggestive of a cup final than an ordinary League match.

The commencement of play was characterised by Halifax showing marked superiority forward and by the referee exacting penalties under the "feet-up " rule. Warrington were the principal sufferers, and at times one felt inclined to doubt the justice of Mr M'Cutcheon's decisions. There was so much screwing of ths pack by the home forwards that the men were always on the move, and they had either to utilise their feet or sit down. The repeated possession of the ball which Halifax obtained gave them the upper hand for some time and Warrington were forced to defend. On the attack the Halifax men were vigorous but not very scientific, and their straight across passing was easily checked by the more speedy Warrington backs. Still it was some time before the visitors found their feet, i.e. got the measure of the home forwards and their peculiar methods. Then several incursions into Halifax territory were noted, and once it seemed certain that Hockenhall and Harris would manage a try between them, but they spoiled the opening after a clever run• Warrington's period on the attack was not very lengthy as a rule, for Little's hue punts with the breeze gener- ally landed the ball well in the Warrrington quarter. Before half-time Halifax had been twice very near scoring, Once when Joe Riley tried to dash over at the corner after a series of scrums on the line, and again when Bartle charged Knight's kick, but was held by Fish on the verge of the rut.

In the second half Warrington showed marked super- iority, and kept the homesters almost continually on the defence. The backs were repeatedly on the move, but the tackling on the other side was vigorous and effec- tive Fish, Isherwood and Dickenson all came within an ace of getting through, the first-named reaching the corner on several occasions only to be bundled in touch. The Warrington forwards were now playing in magni- ficent form and but for one or two stoppages I think they would have run their heavier opponents to a stand- still. Time after time Burgess and. Hockenhall got possession and set the threequarter line going, but to no purpose. Penalties relieved the Halifax line on several occasions when it seemed as if the attack must prevail, and the" blue and whites" must be accounted lucky to escape.

But they had better luck to follow. During a brief visit to the Warrington quarter another penalty was awarded, and Little took his fourth shot at goal, the ball "crossing the bar" to the accompaniment of deafening cheers. There were only six valuable minutes of time left, and such a reverse was enough to have disheartened most teams, but Warrington were in no despairing mood- They dropped out in a twinkling and were soon hammering away again at the home defenen nuckenhall twice punted trickily to the corner for Fish, and it seemed once that the winger was over,but no ! Joe Riley was the stumbling block once more, and inches only saved Halifax. Things ‘iot desperate and then the unexpected hippenedq The irre,oressible Burgess got hold from a scrum near touch and dropped—the ball s,iling across the goal from our point of view, but the sudden leap of the ,Warrington- ians and the dead silence of 9,000 people proclaimed the fact that the Flixton youth had really done the trick. It was quite a dramatic reversal of positions, and War- rington tried hard for another point, but time was too short, the match ending in a draw two minutes later.

The Halifax folk were keenly disappointed, but they had to admit that Warrington well-deserved the point they got. Up to that moment Warrington never had a single chance at goal, while Little himself was given four opportunities, so that the balance of Fortune's favours had certainly been on the home side. It would only have been a fair result had Warrington just won, for on the whole, they were the better side. Halifax are undoubtedly a good team, not brilliant, but sound and reliable in every department, with a great fund of energy and dash. Probably neither side was seen at its best, but it was a great game, fairly and squarely fought, and full of interesting play. There was only a moderate use of touch,both teams playing open football and the display, considering the keenness of the encounter, could hardly have been improved upon.

It was a match in which not a man on either side played badly. Joe Riley, who came in as substitute for Wedgwood on the right wing, was the best of the home quartette, and came nearer to scoring than any of the others, while his covering of Fish was admirably effective. There are not many•wings who could have kept Fish at bay so continuously as Riley did on Satur- day. Rigg and Hadwen played well, the latter being always reliab'e and neat in his work. Mosley was the best of the halves, but showed the same fault as last year—a disinclination to be held when fairly tackled— which tends to rough play, and is certainly against the best interests of the game. Little was also in fine form but Warrington frequently caught him napping with cross-punting. By making him run for the ball they often got him down and prevented a huge kick. The forwards were very fine both in the scrum and the open. but on the day's play not a bit superior to the 'Warring- ton lot, who were admirably led by Forster, Morrison, Roberts, and boardman. Warrington's backs were all on a par, though I have seen Fish field the ball better, and Hockenhall at times ran too far across before part- ing with:the ball. Knight again played a good game and showed plenty of pluck in sticking to his work after twice being badly damaged. If I remember right Burgess's goal was only the third he has dropped since he joined the Warrington club. The first was in his opening match against Salford at Warrington, the second against Leigh last Christmas day, and since then he has been lying low— so to speak —coming out of his shell in startling fashion on Saturday. It would have been difficult to find an individual more pleased with himself than was Burgess when in the dressing-room after the match. He deserved all the lusty pats on the back that he get too!

The Lancashire and Cheshire match at Runcorn will doubtless attract a good number of Warringtonians to-day, seeing that Fish and Boardman are doing duty for the County Palatine. The Cestrians have by no means so poor a chance of victory as would seem to be the case on paper,and playing on the Irwell lane ground will give them additional confidence. Last season Cheshire were the Champion county, and they again aspire to the honour.

I hope the absence of Fish and Boardman from the Warrington fifteen will not make all the difference between winning and losing to the homesters. Fish's absence from the Salford match undoubtedly caused Warrington's defeat, but then the team was further disorganised by Dickenson being on the injured list. I To-day with Edmunds in place of Fish, and J Joolley as substitute for Boardman, the team should be good enough to account for Leigh, especially on the Wilders- pool ground. Leigh are very cocky this season, but I tang there is not the same class about the rear division as is possessed by Warrington, and with Molyneux a pos-;ible absentee the homesters should prove their superiority.

I have a bit of news for the crowd to-day. Warring- ton are turning out in their brand-new jerseys, which must, of course, be honoured by a win. The colours are the same • but the " bars " are running across inste dof downward, and the new togs" are likely to give the team a very smart appearance

The "A "team on Saturday easily trounced the second string from Birkenhead, and some of our juniors showed considerable smartness. H. Watkins scored three tries, Brook and Burton also playing an improved game. W. Hind, who having given a trial at half back also made a promising debut.

The CHAIRMAN invited Mr Crosfheld to distribut the prizes which he had kindly presented. Mr Caomeen,who was coedially rec, ived on rising tee make the distributioe, said they sometimes sandwiched in a little bit of " stumping " on occasions of this kind, and be supposed the music, the songs, and the rest ot the entertainment were a sort of gilding for the political pill. (Laughter.) One was tempted to say a good deal, but as they were soon to° have their annual meetinz at the club he would not keep them long before proceeding with the regular business of the evening. He advised every one present who had followed the correspondence in the heal newspapers on the Education Bill to read the vary important and interesting letter by their presi- dent, Mr Parker, which he had read in the train on his way to the meeting. That gentleman had the gift of putting plain and homely facts in a way that they could be " understended of the people." and it was a gift as important nowadays as it was when their old friend, Abraham Lincoln, laid such stress on it in America. And certainly in the valuable letters Mr I Parker had written on the Elucation Bill—a very intricate questiete—he had helped to bring home some of the more important facts in a way that I must strike not aloha specialists, but every man of common sense who considered tee ,s we invelved He (Mr Croifield) was not going to treat the audience to any long discussion either upon the Education Bill or upon anything else, because his duty was to distribute ithe prizee. He was always glad to see that at bowls and billiards the club continued to flourish. That side of the club's work wao doing uncommonly well, and he hoped it would continue to do en, as every side of the I institution was a nursery for Liberal opinion in the town. (Applause.) He trusted also that it would be more and more a focus and a centre where active Liberale en would be developed pare passu, and that the club might in the long run aff erd the assoeiatiou more assistance, support, and backing than it had been able to do hitherto. Applause). Mr CROSIFIKLD then distributed the prizes as follows : 1, silver-plated tea set, R Marrow ; 2, gold signet ring and barometer, J Davies; 3, case of cutlery,G H Shaw; 4, six-bottle cruet. R Kerr ; 5. geld brooch, A J Jones : 6, prize selectee, W Berton ; 7, cake basket, A Green- loslgh ; 8, cigarette case, C Jordan 9, silver-plated teapot, J Berry ; 10, case of carvers, A livneketne ; 11, silver-plated bnakfast cruec, E J Mitchell ; 12, silver- plated jam disb and spoon, F Baker. THE PRESENTATION.

COUNCILLOR TINNION AND HIS CANDIDATURE. Councillor TINNION said he had a very important ano very pleasant duty to perform, but before doing it he hoped the audience would excuse him if he referred to , his candidature in St Austin's ward. As they were doubtless aware he (Mr Ticiaioa) was to be oppoted. He did not grumble at Chat; be thought he tiad been a lighter ever since he came to Warrington and he was not likely to grumble because be had an opportunity of fighting now. He understood that his opponent was to be Mr Lord. ' He bad the pleasure of meeting Mr Lord in Bridge-street, the other day, when he he beard he was likely to come out, and he thought the best thing he could do was to eanvass him for leis vote on his (Mr 'Donlon's) behalf. (Liughtar.) Mr Lord told him he bad been invited by the Non-Trading Committee to oppose him (Mr Tinnion), and that the association had offered to pay his expenses. Mr Lord added that be was intimately connected with the Noc-Trading Aso CiatiOrl and had taken a prominent part in connection with the agitation. Mr Lord asked him (Mr Tinniou) how he stood in that matter and he replied that he did not quarrel with the non-tit...den or their object, but that he differed very materially with their methods. (Hear, hear). He (Mr TinniOn) expected to hear of Mr Lord appearing on the platform of the Non-Trading Committee on Thursday evening next at Parr Hall if he etuck to his guns. That was his position. Certainly tte speaker would stand to his guns ails he now stood before the public as the representative of what he considered to be hie honest, conscientious and straightforward services on behalf o/ the ratepayers particularly on behalf of the ratepa,yers of St Austin's Ward. He would not shirk the issue with the Nen. Trading Association, and he was prepared to place the issue fairly before the electors, but was it absolutely necessary for a man to be honest that he should be be attached- becly and soul to the Non-Trading Committee ? (A Voice, "Certainly not.") He was prepared to face the issue and say he represented honesty and consistency, that he had no axe to grind, and that he had not even turned the grinding stone for anyone else. (Applause.) What he had done he had done honestly, and from conviction, and he had never been ashamed by voice and vote to oppose what he thought was dot in the best interests of Warrington. (Armhole.) Flo was not afraid of the result of the elee- tion,and as the result of hia canvass he had every reason to believe that Isis majority would be. the largest that ever any man had received at the hands of tee electors of Warrington. That morning he found from the local newspapers that Mr Lord was to come out aseithe Con- servative candidate for St:. Austin's Ward, aCcl he (the speaker) left the people of Warrington to reconcile Mr LJed's position. He appreciated the considerat,o a he had always received at the hands of the Conservative patty. He declined to believe the Genre rvative party would be dragged at the tail of the Non-Frading party, and he believed they had the SIMS opinion of him as many of the Liberals and other ratepayers had of such men as Councillors John Roberts, Joseph Shillcock, A .1 Jolley and Arthur Bennett, who were not men who had been sent to the Council purely for their political opinions. He should be sorry if they were going to revert to the old system of electing men solely and purely for their political opinions. Men should be elec- ted for their worth and net because they were either Liberal or Tory. (Applause). He wai proud to be a Liberal in politics, but he would not flout his opinions in front of everyoae. He would not be bound by an; party and go to the Council simply as a delegate. but as a free and independent representative professing Liberal opinions. He believed the best part of the Conserva- tive party at any rate would give him credit for being as useful as the gentleman he had named. Councillor Tinnion then alluded to the candidature of Couoeillor James Evans and Mi s3rs Brophy and Upson who, he said, had done consider Ole service to the Liberal party. He appealed to these present to give them their hearty support. He felt sure that with such a band of.. workers there was not the slightest doubt hut that every Liberal candidate would be returned by a very handsome majority. (Applause.) That was not the object for which he rose. The object was a very pleasant one, and that was to propos!, the health of the President, Mr Crosfield, the doaor of the handsome prizes on the table. He spoke of the donor in eulogistic terms, and said that of all the illus noes names War- rington had ever known the name of Crosfleld stood out the foremost. (Applause.) Their President was a noble representative of a noble family. If Warrington only knew his true worth—it took time to show true worth to the world—it would return him, if he wished to stand, in the Liberal interest as the member for the borough. (Applause.) He now wished to present Mr Ciceefield in the name of the members with the handsome work of art they saw befcre them. It Was a matter of dispute, whetter photography was an art, but in hi opinion, looking at the beautiful picture Mr Birtles had pro. duced,it was an excellent work of art. The photograph contained as many members of the club as could possibly assemble on the Maturdar afternoon on which the main took place. He would like to add that the idea of a presentation did not spring from the com- mittee but it was a spontaneous gift from the regular members of the club. It was simply to show the cordial appreciation of the members. On their ; behalf he had now touch pleasure in asking Mr Croafield !

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS:-
div.p: THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS:-
TORIES IN A FIX.
LIVELY MEETING OF THE CONSERVATIVE COUNCIL. MR. JOHN WHITE FAILS TO SWALLOW MR. PEMBERTON.
MR. LORD'S CANDIDATURE DISAPPROVED.

A special and important meeting of the Council of the Warrington Conservative Association was held in the Assembly Room, Cmservative Club, on Tuesday even- ing. Oa the previous Friday Mr John Lord had been selected by the St Austin's Ward Committee to oppose Councillor 'Finnion in the Conservative interest. The only business of the meeting was to con- sider the following resolution, to be moved by Mr John White, the Chairman of the Association :—" That the nomination of Mr John Lori for St Austin's Ward be not confirm,d " Naturally this resolution aroused much interest, and it is not surprising that the attendance was large. Mr John White presided.

div.head: MR._ JOHN WHITE SPEAKS PLAINLY.
div.p: MR._ JOHN WHITE SPEAKS PLAINLY.

Mr JOHN WHITE SAid he wou-i—d—h—a;e -13-e-e—n—g.l;:d-.to have escaped the duty he had before him that eveoing,but be had never attempted to shirk his duty, and however un- Pleasant it might be he meant to go through to the end. He should have to speak at eonsid.rable length

div.head: IT AUGHT BE FOR THE LAST TIME.
div.p: IT AUGHT BE FOR THE LAST TIME.

(Cries of "N, no.") Toe t'rne had---arriCe-d-When sorn:- one mui.t speak out, and speak plainly too. Be had taken no advantage of any one as regarded Vie resolution on the notice paper, for be had tak4n good care that evf ryone should know what he intended to do. There- fore in sending out the notice convening the meeting he put plainly before thr m its objects and intentions. Be had often spoken to them in that room, never at great length, because he always wished to try to draw others out. Be had alwats spoken in the most conciliatory way, but he was afraid his observations that evening would be neither conciliatory nor pleasant ; but they must boar with him even if the remarks he had to make appeind not to be very relevant to the quesion. Be would like to refer them to the history of the Conserva- tive Association for the past 22 years. It was in the year 1880 that he first became convinced of the fact that some drastic measures were necessary if the Con servative Association and the Cmservative pirty wore to be in the ascendency in Warrington. With that

div.head: MISERABLE AND WRETCHED DEFEAT
div.p: MISERABLE AND WRETCHED DEFEAT

at the hands of the Halical party in 1880. when Mr MeMinnies was return.d by a maj)rity of 529, many of the Conservatives felt they had been too apathetic, and that the time bad arrived when they ought to be up and doing. (Applause ) H 3 became the treasurer at a time when the As aoeiation was £5OO or £6OO in debt. They knew what an important factor finance played in connection with an association.. At that time they had a poor miserable club in Academy- street, but now they had their present spacious and comfrtabl, building. (Applause.) At the time to wh'ch he alluded they bad no Conservative newspader. They had no r o definitely appointed Conner', everything was haphazard. Now they had properly drawn up rules and an organizel Council, and whit had bleu the result ? They had Lola from one vic- tory to another, until at the last Parliamentary election they culminated in a magnificent majority for the Cori- aervative candidate of over 1,000. (Applause). He did not take credit himself for all this. The result lay with them and not with hiFe. They had worked earnestly and unitedly at all the elections, and it had brought about the state of things to which he had referred. They had been the main factors in these results, and unless they had supported the party the latter would not have been in the poaition in which it stood that day. (Hear, hear). Through all this he bad striven for unity, without which all their efforts would be in vain, and they had that unity until a year ago

div.head: WHEN MR. PEADIEHTON APPEARED ON THE SCENE
div.p: WHEN MR. PEADIEHTON APPEARED ON THE SCENE

He was glad Mr Pemberton was present. He should not have liked to say whit he WRI3 about to say in his atssnce, but he said that Mr Pemberton had broken up the Conservative party in Latehford Ward. He did not complain of that—they bad berm a party to it—but not content with that they must attempt to break up the party in St Austin's Ward. This might appear to the meting to ba very stroog loneuage, and no doubt Mr Pemberton would be anery with him, but he could not help saying what he thought, and that was that—as long as their unity was perfect they carried everything before them, so that if their unity was to be destroyed the association and the Conservative patty would be destroyed. (Hear, hea,..) He (the Chairman) had no axe to grind. Be stood before them that evening with no axe to grind or ambition to satisfy except one ambition, and that was to maintain the success of the Conservative pirty and its ascendency in the town. (Apn,ause.) But he could do that no longer, and alas, would

div.head: SEE HIS FACE NO MORE.
div.p: SEE HIS FACE NO MORE.

He had said that their unity was in danger, and he had taken upon himself to blame one member of the associa- tion more than another for it. He was sorry but what were the facts ? They would say "What has this to do with Mr Lord ? " That gontlenian came to him a month ago, and told him that he was in a position to be ths candidate for St Austin's Ward. He (the chairman)did not know Mr Lord. He had never seen or heard of bins but•if he had bsen a prominent Conservative he should have heard of him, He had his doubts about him, and accordingly decided to make inquiries from three differ- ent sources and he was told that Mr Lord was a Radical. He made inquiries from three different and independent FOoIC'S. In the course of time Mr Lord came again tosee him and with him came his friend, the inevitable Mr Pemberton. He (Mr White) said to Mr Lord, " Well. Mr Lord, you are a Radical," and the reply was "No, I am not. I am a Conservative and I have never voted Radical since I came to Warrington." He replied to Mr Lord, " All my information goes to prove the fact that von are a Radical, and the people I have asked are people I can depend upon. Under he circumstances I cannot give you any encouragement to centest the ward." Mr Lord again said that hs was not a Radical. He added, " Mr Pemberton will tell you I am not a Radical, and he (Mr White) said" I must be'ieve what you say, but I have another objection, and that is that you are a metro- her of the Municipal Non-Trading Association, and I am not going to be a party to any one who wants to farther the interests of the Municipal Non-Trading Association." Mr PEMBERTON (int =irrupting) : Is this true ? Mr Lord said to me that you had said that Mr Ashcroft had a prior claim. Mr Lord then said that "ir that is so I shall willingly work for Mr Ashcroft and give him £5 towards the expenses." Is that so ? The CHAIRMAN : That is quite correcl% Continuing his speech, Mr WHITE said they now came to the Munici- pal Non-Trading Association. That would be a delicate subject, and no doubt there were several gentlemen in the hall who upheld and fell in With the views of that Association. With their private views he had nothing to do, and all he wished to say about the

MUNICIPAL NON-TRADING ASSOCIATION was this—that in all their endeavours they were honest, and really believed and thought what they said and did. But what he wanted to say for his own part wag this,that heihadjno sympathy with the rn thods they em- ployed or the language they used. So far as the Corpora- tion were conserned he was the'last man to stand up for them because nearly all his professional life he bad been antagonistic to them in business matters. Continually had he been corresponding on business matters, such as the laying out of streets, the sale of property, and on all these occasions he had quarrelled with them severely. But this he would say, that in all the doings he bad had witts them, the officials, from the highest', to the lowest, had shown thg greatest interest in Warrinetou, and had done the best thy could for the town, Therefore he would b no party to sti.anatising and vilifying men who had given their time and services to the boroutth all these years. kliear bear). They could not do two things at once. They could not run the association as A plitical asso;istion, find political candi lates, and can• didsteS for the Municipal Non-Trading Association. If they did so they would wreck the Conservative Associa- sion. They saw what had taken 1.1 we already in three wards, and what had happened in three wards wouH banner) in all the others. (Hear, hear). They 000ld not work the two forces together, and he for one was not going to see the Conservative issociation

div.head: DRAGGED THROUGH TECE MUD
div.p: DRAGGED THROUGH TECE MUD

at the heels of the Municipal Non-trading Association. (Applause.) That was what it amounted to. Mr Lord might be a Conservative—he did not say he was not— but he was a member of the Municipal Non-Tradini:; Association, and he asserted that he, instigated by Mr Pemberton and his association, was coining out to use the Conservative Association to attain his ends. (Herr, hear, and aunt iuse.) He (Mr White) would not be a party to that, and if members of the Council present perilsted in that course a-id sanctioned it by their votes that night,they would be hying the foundation for snlitting up,tbe Conservative Association. (Applause.) He should I,lre to point out what they were losing sight of—that they existed unmanly for one great duty, and thal: was to return a Conservative to Parliament. That was their duto and everything else was subservient to it. (applause.) If be returning Conservatives to the Council they could achieve thatobject they would return Conservatives, but if by having these contests every November they split the party into factions they did more harm than good. It had often been said that there ought to be no politics introduced into the Coun- cil chamber. He quite agreed, and he shoul I be thank- ful that these horrible November elections, so far is politics were concerned, should be done away with. He had been sick and tired of them for years. But they could not help themselves. They had been driven into a corner, and if anyone could show a way out of it he Elhould be thankful, but at priosent they could not. Mr Pilling had said that ward meetings were a farce. He (the speaker) believed they were a farce in this way —that the members of the ward who should meet to select the candidates did not turn up. It was no use bringing forward a candidate that was unpopular. That happened in Latchford. He was sorry to say that Mr Pemberton was not popular. He was a hard-working man, but he was not popular. He might have found that out last year when they had the unhappy spectacle

of a lot of Conservatives voting for a Radical, and this year a still more curious spectacle of a lot of Liberals voting for a Conslroativs. That went to show that there was something wrong sornewnere, and that the ward committees ought to take more inter:st in their work and bring forward a candidate who would be fairly popular. He did not say that a man could please all.but he should boa man who was reasonably popul ir Mr Pemberton had not pleased the majority, sal it would have been bet;er if he had not come out again. I He (Mr White) had had to swallow many things arid to put up with a good deal of inconveoience, which he did not mind, and give up a great deal of his time, which ha did not mind. He had been called upon to settle petty grievances which ought not to nave arisen and swallow a good many unpleasant things. He tried last week to

SWALLOW MR. PEMBERTON, and he thought be bad swallowed him, but they knew what happened when they swallowed a thin.; that del not agree with them. lie would net enter into detailq. but he had thrown Mr Pemberton up, and why ? Becinae although he might have stood him as the can- didate for Latchford, coming forward as he did, and being carried as he. was last week, yet when be found he Was playing the same game in Sr. Austin's Ward he said, " I nave had enough of him, and I thiesw him up." He (Mr White) did nor know what would b 3 the result of the meeting that night, but he asked them to put their foot down as a political body and say they would either abstain from elections altogether, or if they chose anyone they [mould be bona-fide Coeiserva- fives. (Applause). They had now arrived at a crisis ,in the history of the party, and he hoped they would take the matter seriously to heart. fie should be sorry if the unity of the party Was broken up. Ile hoped sin- cerely that he had said something to prevent that catastrophe, and 'shat when the first of November was over tt.i year ad their little differences would be for- gotten, and that they would work together as a united party determined to maintain their position in the town which they had won through suel arduous fights during the last 20 years. He uo ,osrl r,n resel ion :--" That the nomination ot M . Join L for 6,. Austin's Ward be not confirmed." (Applause).

Mr C S BURGESS 4.C;o,lided. i'ney had tn-t as Con- setvitive., and for Muoicipal Dion- Craders to try to get into the Town Council through the Conservative party WSB neither fair nor honourable. (Hear, hear.) Mr J MARRATT supported. Mr ASHCROFT : Who are to s2lect the candidat,,s—the executive or the association ?

The CHAIRMAN AS long as the rules are AS they arp the Ward Committees, subject to the confirmation of this meeting. Mr ASHCROFT ald he Wee a Cmiservative,but he would not have his hands tied if he had views the other way. He WAS not a member of the Municipal Nm-Crading, Association.

MR. PEMBERTON WITH HIS BACK TO THE WALL Mr JOBN PEMBERTON said that a reference had been made to tnii decision of the electors of the Latchford Ward, and it had been said by the Cnairrnan that it was patent he was not a popular candidate. But who could have got the same number of votes he got under the , circumstances ? (" No one.") Be had been a‘member of the club ever since it had been built, when Mr Speak- man was the manager, and he was manager long before the Municipal Non-Trading Association was t!"10U4Ot of. lie learnt his Conservatism in Liverpool, where every- thing appertain .n; to Ceaservatism was honest, straightforward and above board. He was sorry to say ha had not had that treatment in Warringtou. It had been said that he was using tbe club to further the Municipal Nm-Tradiag Associa- tion, but he had not called upon the association to pay anything for him. He had always paid every farthing of his txpenses, and that was what many a prominent member of the associa- tion had not done; there was no doubt that the facts had been misrepreseuted to Mr White, and he believed that if he know the truth, tie whole truth, of the agita- tion against him he would not be a party to it for a moment. (Hear, hoar.) He had met Mr White in business and had known him for many years, and every- thing be had done had been done straightforwardly and honestly. Mr White had heard all things said against him, but he did not know of them of his own know- ledge. What oroof had Mr White that these things were true? Mr Wtoite bad said that Mr Lord was not a Conservative. Who had told him so? Could they find a betr Conservative than Me L ord ? Mr Tinnion was la Liberal but, $ ienainely, he had many friends present. lln regard to his own election he had been surprised I with the remarksthat had fallen from the Chairman. He had a desire to become a member of the Council before the Non-Municipal Trading Association was thought of. They bad been unfair in not giving him al opportunity to meet the people who had made those charges against him. When he first thought of becoming a can- didate for Latchford Ward he was told someone had a prior claim, and he bowed to the decisirms of the club and party. When he did fight on fought the strongest man that could be fought in the ward. He did not wait for a "walk over" like some people did, tie did not think any Conservative in the Council had had such hearty workers as he had,as the result proved. With the treat- ment, however, that had been extended to him over the present matter did they wonder that they did not get prominent men to come and represent the Conservatives in the Town Council ? If he had not the interest of the ratepayers at heart did they:think he would wallow in that dirt P He had nothing to gain by it. It had been Said that he was

GOING INTO THE TOWN COUNCIL TO SELL BRICKS. (Laughter.) Whether they believed that he did no kaow but considering the firm he was connected with was a private one he could not sell anything to the Corpora- tion without being subj icted to a penalty of £5O, and he thought he had too many friends on the Corporation to allow him to sell 53 wo VI. (Laughter.) That educated men believed the rumours that had gained currency surprised him beyond expression. Were had he attempted to cause a split in the party ? Reverting to the Latchford Ward, he said after offering his sere ces he waited until the committee selected him, and in the meantime the non-municipal trading movement started. And what were its objects ?To purify public life. He had had to suffer persecution from men in that MOM who called them4elves good Conservatives, and yet he had never left the club. Pe put it down that the indivi- duals who did it were responsible,and not the principles of the party. Because he wanted to purify public life could not he be a good Conservative ? (Hear, hear ) He asked, and be thought he had a right to demand it, that before the facts went forward from that meeting he should have a chance of answering the accusations that had ben made• He did not think people should go behind bis 'back and teil the Chairman any tale they liked, and he asked him to extend that justice which he hoped to receive from the committee. (Applause) In no election had be bad the aid of the Liberal party at his back. He did not know whether that carried weight, but he should think it spoke volumes to an ordinary man. (Applause.) Mr W J WILSON—Whit course is this association going to take with regard to Mr Pemberton in the Latchford Ward. The CHAIRMAN —That has been settled. Whatever support is given by the Association to the ()Ulm be will receive

Mr WILSON observed that when Mr Pemberton came forward Mr Pilling did not open his mouth against him. Judge of his (Mr Wilson's) surprise when Mr Pilling got up and proposed another candidate, and Mr Jolley seconded—both non-voters in the L ttchford Ward. A great deal of that trouble and grievance had totien brought about through the heads of the partr not taking a title more interest in their work. He contended that Mr Pilling had not been open with his committee, and that he took a moan way to achieve his end. He could assure them that he would always stand loyal to Mr White, who, porhaps, might have been led astray in regard to Mr Pemb,rton. lie thought in justice to Mr Pemberton that those who had made charges against him should la t brought to face him. (Applause). If the association were ving to support him he would do so. If not he would hot. But what would they have done if he had done the same thing as Mr Pilling Would they have moved that his name be erased from the membership of the association ? If they were going to support Mr Pemberton, then Mr Pilling, according to the rules, had no right to raise a haad on behalf of Mr W B oberts. (Applaus-). If they were going to sup- port Mr PPmberton he would call upon them to put the rules and regulations of the association into full force. Mr PE:ASEBI.IN said he was tak tn back by the attack which had unexpectedly been made upon him and

NOT BEING USED TO PUBLIC SPEAKING— The CHAIRMAN:—Not being used to what ? (Laugh- ter.) Mr. PEMBERTON replied that he had never spoken from a public platferm befcre doing So at the Parr Hall. The CII&IRMAN:—You made a very good start. Mr PEMBERTON:—I am much obliged to you for your favourabll criticism. Continuing, he said it had been spread out in the ward by prominent Cmseroatives and members of that association, that he was a Liberal. He did not think that ought to be allowed. He did not wish to mention any names, but the people were present and knew. He had been to two peoVe to ask them to sign his nomination papers, when he was told that So- and-40 had said he wa a Liberal. He thought the Chairman ought to extend his kindly help in trying to stop that sort of thing. Councillor GREENING supported the resolution and thanked the Chairman for the strocce rnsitinn he had taken that evening. The Conservative cause in War- rington required, and had, at present, a strnog and fairiminded man at its bead, and he was sorry to hear Mr. MIMI say that might be the last time he would be in the position of chairman. If that was so Conserva- tism in Warrington would meet with a great calamity, but heboped Mr. White would re-consider the matter. 11 ALDERMAN SUTTON'S VIEWS. Aidermln SUTTON said it was unanimously agreed at the ward meeting that Mr Lord should be their candi date. He (Alr Sutton) had act ed impartially as chair man of the ward meeting, a nd everything wa dons fairly and above board. He agreed tha ward meetings had proved, of late, altogethe • mistake. It should not be left to a very few members to select a candidate for the ward, and sooner or later it would be well to re-consider the

rule of the association bearing up an that point. They ought to select a man who met will, as far as possible, the approval of every member of the association.ftegard hag the question of non-traders, he believed it was much better if they had no connection with them at al,. (Hear, hear.) They were perfectly justified, if they thougut fit, Co meet at Farr Hall and denounce the mem- bers of the Corporation for improper conduct. He quite agreed, in fact, he nal often said tnat it was a pity the ratepayers did not take m)re intercst in what was going on in the Town Council than they bad done, but he objected to anycne coming there from a distance villifyiag members of the Corpo-atioa, wliom they had never known in their life—members who had just as irreproachable characters s they had themselves. If they would go to the C -ranch and ask for informa- tion respecting anything that took pito% he bad no doubt they-would get all the inform ition that it was possible t givethern. If they wanted to gat at • certain party or rnemher of the Corcnration for having done what they cmsid -red was not correct, or moral, they bad no right to attack every inernher of the Council for having been guilty of conduct which was not at all weer. That was the reason why be, as a member of the association, objected to anyone coming forward and trying to become a reprekntative of the ratepayers. In his opinion they did not altogether come as remeieatatives of the rat !payers, but to air their own grievances. (Applause.) The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried by 37 votes to 5.

div.head: BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, RUNCORN.
div.p: BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, RUNCORN.

Th. annual choir sermons were preached on Sunday at Bethesda Congregational Churcn by the Rev y Carter (late of North wich). At the morning service the choir sang the antlem " Jisu word of God incarnate," and in the evening " Abide with me " (the solos of which were taken by Miss Clare, Mr Wornll, and Mr Littler), and "It is high time to awake." At the evening service, the cantata " Esther, the beautiful queen " was given by an augmented choir. The principal characters were taken as follows :—Q.ioen, Miss E Clare ; king, Mr T Johnson ; Mordecai, Ir E Worrell ; Haman, Mr A Shingler ; Z?„rish, Mrs C Lathwocd ; maid of honour, Miss L Stubbs ; Hegar, Mr C Leathwood. The organist was Mr G Pritchard, and the conductor Mr J Holferd (formerly of Runcorn). Collections were taken in aid of the choir fundF.

A SINGULAR POINT. Sequel to a Boy's Death at Rixton. At the Warrington County Celle, en Thursday, George Howard, labourer, Woolston Green, Martinscroft, brought an action against Edward Marshall, farmer, Rixton, to recover £l5O compensation under the Work- men's Compensation Act of 1900 for this loss of bis grandson.—Mr Browne appeared for the applicant, and Mr E A. White represented the respondent. Mr Browne said the boy was killed whilst working on respondent's farm at Riston,at the inquest a verdiot of " Accidental death" was returned. Mr Longton appeared and subsequently entered the present sent proceedings. Applicant brought the claim as being dependent upon the boys earnings. Deceased lived with the applicant and his wages were 6s per week. Mr Longton could not appear in the case that day and had put the matter in his (Mr Browne') 'hands. Respon- dent's reply to the claim was that applicant was not the grandfather of the deceased. It was quite true that the boy was not the legitimate son of his mother and there- fere the mother could not apply, but as the mother was the daughter of the applicant Mr Langton contended that tho applicant was entitled to recover compensa- tion. His Honour ruled against Mr Browse on this point. Mr Browne then applied for an amendment in the form of the application whereby applicant could resovor a corn not eseeeding £lO as the person incurring the expenses of the medical attendance upon and the Innenl of the deceased. This was agreed to, and Mr White raising no objse- tion, his Honour gave judgment for the applicant for £lO. There was some discussion with regard to the question of costs, and applicant Was ultimately awarded El.

Saturday will be a great day for London, and great preparations are being made in consequence. The metropolis has already assumed the holiday garb it has worn for such a considerable part of the present year: and all the stands, which between constant wet .and London grime have entirely lost the newness of June, have been touched up and mt.cle gay for the great procession. If the day is only fine, the result of these manifold preparations will be very bright, and nothing will be lost by the 'postponement from June of this real Coronation tour of the principal parts of the metropolis, to which has been joined the civic reception, which was to have, been given to the King and Queen on July fith. The King returned from Newmarket on Saturday night, and the Queen arrived from Denmark during the course of the week: and all the final arrangements for the procession have been passed. The streets will be lined by some 50,000 troops under the super- vision of General Sir Henry Trotter, commanding the Home District: and Sir Edward Bradford has drawn up a code of special police regulations for the purpose of keeping order and regulating the traffic, which will be stopped soon after nine in the morning. The procession itself will form about noon and start from Buckingham Palace along the route, which has already been published. the King and Queen driving in the new State Carriage, which was built for the original procession of June 27th with a view to giving a better view of their Majesties than is afforded by the State Coach proper. The procession will consist of an advance party of mounted troops and a Naval detachment, followed by batteries of the Royal Horse Artillery, two squadrons of Household Cavalry and the band
